{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],
  "core_four": {
    "context": "Everything the model can see while it works: the repo, files, README instructions, settings. tac-1 keeps context deliberately tiny — one file and two directories — so the difference between the two prompts is unmissable.",

# Elite Context Engineering
**Lesson #9 (Intermediate)**  ·  https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/rd-framework-context-window-mastery

_A focused agent is a performant agent. The context window is your agent's most precious resource - ephemeral, limited, and critical to success. Master context engineering through the R&D Framework._

## Loot Box — 18 notes

### 🔥 Context Engineering: The Name of the Game
A focused agent is a performant agent. Context engineering is the name of the game for high value engineering in the age of agents. Context is a critical in-agent leverage point that determines how an agent performs at any given task.

### 🔥 Four Levels of Context Engineering
There are three levels of context engineering and a fourth hidden level if you're on the bleeding edge pushing into agentic engineering. Master all four levels to achieve complete context window mastery.

### 🔥 Context Sweet Spot Range
There's a sweet spot - a range of context where your agent performs to its maximum possible capability for the task at hand. As you scale to hundreds and thousands of agent executions, hitting this sweet spot consistently becomes even more important.

### 🔥 Hit the Core Four Bullseye
When aligned with the right model, prompt, tools, and the right range of context, we can hit the core four bullseye over and over. This directly increases our agentic coding KPIs and tells us if we're improving our capabilities.

### 🔥 Search and Destroy Context Bloat
Search and destroy is the real skill in context engineering. The real trick is finding context agentically and then removing and delegating context so it doesn't create context rot and context bloat.

### 🔥 Reduce and Delegate Context
There are only two ways to manage your context window: R and D - reduce and delegate. Every technique fits into one or both of these buckets.

### 🔥 Context Window: Precious & Temporal Resource
Your agent's context window is a precious, renewable, but limited temporal resource. It's ephemeral, resets, and is alive for only a certain amount of time. The state in your context window is critical to your success.

### 💎 What Gets Measured Gets Managed
Whenever you have a resource that determines your success, you must measure it so you can improve it. The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding.

### ⚔️ Elite Context Engineering Repository
git clone https://github.com/disler/elite-context-engineering.git

### ⚙️ Measure Context Window State
/context

### 🔥 Avoid Vibe Coding
If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit, which is already a massively saturated space.

### 🔥 Install Token Counter in IDE
Install a tokenizer right in your IDE so you know what's coming into your agent's context. Token counters help you understand context consumption before files are loaded into your agent.

### 🔥 Avoid MCP Server Bloat
Do not load MCP servers unless you need them. Default .mcp.json files can consume 10-12% of your entire context window, completely wasted unless you're actively using every single MCP server. Be very purposeful with your MCP servers.

### 🔥 Delete Default .mcp.json Files
Get rid of default .mcp.json files completely. Don't use a default .mcp.json for your code base. This immediately clears up your context window and prevents wasteful token consumption on every agent instance.

### ⚙️ Load Specific MCP Server
claude --mcp-config path/to/specific-mcp.json

### 🔥 Context Priming Over Memory Files
Use context priming over claude.md or similar auto-loading memory files. Context priming uses dedicated reusable prompts (custom slash commands) to set up your agent's initial context specifically for the task type at hand, avoiding bloated memory files.

### 🔥 Problems with Always-On Context
Always-on context like claude.md files is not dynamic or controllable. Engineering work constantly changes, but memory files only grow. Eventually they become bloated with irrelevant context, and in worst case, contradictory information.

### ⚙️ Context Priming Command
/prime Agentic Engineer Master AI Coding, AI Agents, and Agentics to build 'living' software Blogs Pi Coding Agent: The Only Claude Code Competitor Top 2% Agentic Engineering The Agent Thread Framework State of AI Coding Compute Advantage Resources Home Account Tactical Agentic Coding Principled AI Coding YouTube Terms Privacy

# Elite Context Engineering
**Lesson #9 (Intermediate)**  ·  https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/rd-framework-context-window-mastery

_A focused agent is a performant agent. The context window is your agent's most precious resource - ephemeral, limited, and critical to success. Master context engineering through the R&D Framework._

## Loot Box — 18 notes

### 🔥 Context Engineering: The Name of the Game
A focused agent is a performant agent. Context engineering is the name of the game for high value engineering in the age of agents. Context is a critical in-agent leverage point that determines how an agent performs at any given task.

### 🔥 Four Levels of Context Engineering
There are three levels of context engineering and a fourth hidden level if you're on the bleeding edge pushing into agentic engineering. Master all four levels to achieve complete context window mastery.

### 🔥 Context Sweet Spot Range
There's a sweet spot - a range of context where your agent performs to its maximum possible capability for the task at hand. As you scale to hundreds and thousands of agent executions, hitting this sweet spot consistently becomes even more important.

### 🔥 Hit the Core Four Bullseye
When aligned with the right model, prompt, tools, and the right range of context, we can hit the core four bullseye over and over. This directly increases our agentic coding KPIs and tells us if we're improving our capabilities.

### 🔥 Search and Destroy Context Bloat
Search and destroy is the real skill in context engineering. The real trick is finding context agentically and then removing and delegating context so it doesn't create context rot and context bloat.

### 🔥 Reduce and Delegate Context
There are only two ways to manage your context window: R and D - reduce and delegate. Every technique fits into one or both of these buckets.

### 🔥 Context Window: Precious & Temporal Resource
Your agent's context window is a precious, renewable, but limited temporal resource. It's ephemeral, resets, and is alive for only a certain amount of time. The state in your context window is critical to your success.

### 💎 What Gets Measured Gets Managed
Whenever you have a resource that determines your success, you must measure it so you can improve it. The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding.

### ⚔️ Elite Context Engineering Repository
git clone https://github.com/disler/elite-context-engineering.git

### ⚙️ Measure Context Window State
/context

### 🔥 Avoid Vibe Coding
If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit, which is already a massively saturated space.

### 🔥 Install Token Counter in IDE
Install a tokenizer right in your IDE so you know what's coming into your agent's context. Token counters help you understand context consumption before files are loaded into your agent.

### 🔥 Avoid MCP Server Bloat
Do not load MCP servers unless you need them. Default .mcp.json files can consume 10-12% of your entire context window, completely wasted unless you're actively using every single MCP server. Be very purposeful with your MCP servers.

### 🔥 Delete Default .mcp.json Files
Get rid of default .mcp.json files completely. Don't use a default .mcp.json for your code base. This immediately clears up your context window and prevents wasteful token consumption on every agent instance.

### ⚙️ Load Specific MCP Server
claude --mcp-config path/to/specific-mcp.json

### 🔥 Context Priming Over Memory Files
Use context priming over claude.md or similar auto-loading memory files. Context priming uses dedicated reusable prompts (custom slash commands) to set up your agent's initial context specifically for the task type at hand, avoiding bloated memory files.

### 🔥 Problems with Always-On Context
Always-on context like claude.md files is not dynamic or controllable. Engineering work constantly changes, but memory files only grow. Eventually they become bloated with irrelevant context, and in worst case, contradictory information.

### ⚙️ Context Priming Command
/prime Agentic Engineer Master AI Coding, AI Agents, and Agentics to build 'living' software Blogs Pi Coding Agent: The Only Claude Code Competitor Top 2% Agentic Engineering The Agent Thread Framework State of AI Coding Compute Advantage Resources Home Account Tactical Agentic Coding Principled AI Coding YouTube Terms Privacy

1	# TAC-1 · Hello Agentic Coding — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 21:51 · Beginner · Tactic #1: **Stop Coding**
4	> Lesson artifact: a 35-line README, one settings file, and three ~20-line launcher scripts. That's the whole codebase, on purpose.
5	
6	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** AI coding (generating code from prompts) was phase one; agentic coding — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools inside a programmable agent — is phase two, and the engineer who commands it becomes irreplaceable by replacing themselves.
7	
8	**The chapter must land eight ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Idea 1 — A new role exists: the Agentic Engineer
13	
14	**Hook.** In 2023, before it was obvious, Dan bought a domain name as a bet: agenticengineer.com. The bet was that a new software role would emerge, defined not by writing code but by *building systems that can take actions as we can*. Lesson 1 opens by declaring the bet settled: the role now exists, and this course exists to move you into it.
15	
16	**Picture.** Frame t0078 (1:18): the agenticengineer.com page on screen while Dan narrates the 2023 prediction. Frame t0115 (1:55): the two-phase timeline — Phase 1 "AI CODING" (vibe coders born, code commoditized) flowing into Phase 2 "AGENTIC CODING" (real engineers strike back).
17	
18	**Worked example.** The entire lesson repo *is* the role in miniature: nothing in `tac/tac-1` is application code. It's a README of prompts, a permissions file, and launchers — artifacts of someone who directs systems rather than types programs.
19	
20	**Dan's term.** *Phase two Agentic Engineer.* Also the era framing: *"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back."*
21	
22	**Failure mode.** Hearing "new role" as a title change rather than a job change. The weak student keeps doing phase-1 work (prompt → code → paste) with a new label. The role's actual definition — building systems that take actions — is testable: if nothing runs without you pressing the keys, you're still phase one.
23	
24	**Retrieval Q.** What defines the agentic engineer role, in Dan's 2023 prediction wording? *(Building systems that can take actions as we can.)*
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Idea 2 — The mission: become the engineer they can't replace
29	
30	**Hook.** "You know who *they* are. It's your boss. It's the company. It's the industry. It's AI." Nothing in tech is forever — and in a world where your grandma or your little brother can build an app with one prompt, what exactly makes *you* hard to replace?
31	
32	**Picture.** Frame t0124 (2:04): the mission slide. Frame t0162 (2:42): the full-screen **COMMANDER OF COMPUTE** title card — the answer to the question the mission poses.
33	
34	**Worked example.** The answer performed, not stated: by lesson end, a Python script (`programmable/programmable.py`) does a complete branch-write-run-commit-report cycle while the engineer watches. The engineer's contribution moved up one level: they wrote the prompt and the trigger, not the code.
35	
36	**Dan's term.** *Commander of compute* — "We do what we always do in technological revolutions. We move up the stack once again." And the strategy: *build systems that build systems*. The economics: the fabled *10x engineer* comes from 10x **leverage**, never 10x time — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find. Also the end-state: codebases as *self-operating machines* that "literally run themselves."
37	
38	**Failure mode.** Treating the mission as motivational garnish and skipping to the demo. The mission is load-bearing: every later tactic is justified by "does this increase your leverage per unit of attention?" Students who skip it evaluate tactics by comfort instead.
39	
40	**Retrieval Q.** Who are "they" in "an engineer they can't replace," and what is the one-word strategy for becoming that engineer? *(Boss, company, industry, AI; leverage — commanding compute to build systems that build systems.)*
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Idea 3 — Tactic #1: Stop Coding
45	
46	**Hook.** The first tactic is dead simple, mission critical, and potentially uncomfortable. Dan says it twice for complete clarity: **Stop coding.** Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop. This from a man who spent a decade-plus hand-coding at startups and large companies and admits he misses it.
47	
48	**Picture.** Frame t0414 (6:54): the Tactic #1 reveal. The chapter's headline image.
49	
50	**Worked example.** Negative space in the codebase: `tac/tac-1` contains zero hand-written application code, and the course promise is that *throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code gets typed*. `main_aic.py` and `main_tac.py` exist only after an agent creates them.
51	
52	**Dan's term.** *Stop coding.* The supporting cast: "powerful language models [in] agentic loops running on powerful supercomputers are now vastly superior coders than you and I are"; "you're an engineer, not a coder — the difference is massive"; and the reallocation target — *planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures*.
53	
54	**Failure mode.** Two opposite misreadings, both fatal. (a) "No more code" — wrong: code is still a primary asset that generates features and products; you'll generate more than ever. (b) "No more understanding code" — wrong: code understanding remains critically important; review is where your cycles go. And the behavioral failure: agreeing in theory, then hand-editing the agent's output at the first imperfection instead of re-prompting — which trains you to distrust the loop and forfeits the tactic entirely.
55	
56	**Retrieval Q.** Name the two things "stop coding" does NOT mean, and where the freed cycles go. *(Doesn't mean stop generating code or stop understanding it; cycles go to planning, reviewing, closed-loop structures.)*
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Idea 4 — Big Three → Core Four: the one-dimension delta
61	
62	**Hook.** Everything that changed between phase one and phase two is a single added dimension. You already know it — it's been hiding in plain sight, getting more capable over time.
63	
64	**Picture.** Frame t0845 (14:05): the Core Four Venn diagram — CONTEXT (blue), TOOLS (yellow), MODEL (red), PROMPT (green), overlapping over a dimmed view of the lesson README. The one diagram to memorize from lesson 1.
65	
66	**Worked example.** `.claude/settings.json` is the "tools" circle made concrete — the exact tool surface the demo runs on: `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, `Bash(git checkout:*)`, `Bash(git branch:*)`, `Bash(git add:*)`, `Bash(git commit:*)`, `WebSearch`. Read it and you can predict everything the agentic prompt is able to do — and everything it isn't.
67	
68	**Dan's term.** *The big three* (context, model, prompt — "always there even if you can't see it") upgraded by tools to *the core four*. Precise wording matters: the new element is *"prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools."* And the pre-emptive rebuttal to "tool calling isn't new": *"It's not a question of new. It's a question of scale and performance."*
69	
70	**Failure mode.** Shrugging "big whoop, who cares — prompts call tools now" (Dan names this exact shrug). The weak student files the core four as vocabulary instead of as a diagnostic: when an agentic run goes wrong, the cause is always one of the four — wrong context, wrong model, wrong prompt, or wrong/missing tools. Students who internalize it debug systematically; students who don't just re-roll the prompt.
71	
72	**Retrieval Q.** What upgrades the big three to the core four — exact phrasing — and what is Dan's answer to "tool calling isn't new"? *(Prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools; it's not a question of new but of scale and performance.)*
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Idea 5 — Two prompts, one README: AI coding vs agentic coding
77	
78	**Hook.** The lesson's centerpiece is an A/B test you run on your own machine. Same repo, same agent, same afternoon — two prompts. One generates a file. The other does engineering. The difference between them, Dan insists, is *monumental*.
79	
80	**Picture.** Before/after pair: frame t0700 (11:40) — the AI coding prompt creating `main_aic.py`, nothing you haven't seen a million times; frame t0748 (12:28) — Claude Code converting the agentic prompt into a todo checklist; frame t0790 (13:10) — the full trace: `git checkout -b demo-agentic-coding`, `Write(main_tac.py)`, both `uv run` outputs, `git add`, `git commit`, todos checked off.
81	
82	**Worked example.** From `README.md` (35 lines — Dan's count is exact):
83	
84	- **AI Coding Prompt:** `CREATE main_aic.py: print goodbye ai coding` → one file, one print. Phase 1: code generation, full stop.
85	- **Agentic Coding Prompt:** `RUN:` checkout new/existing `demo-agentic-coding` branch → `CREATE main_tac.py:` print "hello agentic coding" + a concise definition of AI agents → `RUN:` `uv run main_aic.py`, `uv run main_tac.py`, `git add .`, `git commit -m "Demo agentic coding capabilities"` → the agent plans, executes step by step, cleans up its todos, reports what it did.
86	
87	Note the prompt's *shape*: RUN/CREATE/RUN reads like a runbook. The prompt is a workflow specification, and the verbs are tool calls.
88	
89	**Dan's term.** *The Agentic (Coding) Prompt* — "a prompt contains a sequence of tool calls." And the observation that unlocks it: "Claude Code is not just writing code. It's calling tools. It's doing engineering work."
90	
91	**Failure mode.** Concluding the prompts are equivalent "because both made files appear." The tell that a student missed the lesson: they can't list what the second prompt did that the first didn't (branch, execute, commit, report). Secondary failure: not rerunning the demo after deleting the branch, so they never see that the workflow is *reproducible* — the property everything in later lessons depends on.
92	
93	**Retrieval Q.** List everything the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't. *(Branch checkout, second file creation per spec, running both programs, git add + commit, todo management + report.)*
94	
95	---
96	
97	## Idea 6 — Why Claude Code: the three essential elements
98	
99	**Hook.** If prompts could always call tools, why did agentic coding only now become real? Because the tools changed and the models improved — and one tool combined the ingredients properly first. There's a new form factor of engineering to take into account.
100	
101	**Picture.** Frame t0903 (15:03): the three-elements slide. Frame t0608 (10:08): the humble on-ramp — VS Code, Cmd+J, `claude`, boot screen.
102	
103	**Worked example.** The demo itself is the evidence: a 12-line prompt produced a plan, five tool executions in the right order with correct recovery of context between them, and a report — with zero baby-sitting. That reliability across a *long chain* is the differentiator the slide names.
104	
105	**Dan's term.** The *three essential elements*: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed; (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools; (3) the right agent architecture. Result: "Reliable agentic coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code." Positioning: "Just as Aider was for the AI coding phase one era, Claude Code represents the best phase two agentic coding tool" — being copied by every other tool. Economics stated plainly: millions and millions of tokens; have the funds or the plan; *pay to play* for maximum ROI. And the anti-lock-in clause: tactics are *transferable* — "don't get stuck on any one tool."
106	
107	**Failure mode.** Tool fixation in either direction: (a) treating the lesson as expired because the UI/models changed — Dan pre-handles this on camera ("your Claude Code UI might look different... that's all great"); (b) fanboy-ing the tool and missing that the three elements are a *checklist for evaluating any agentic tool*, which is the transferable part.
108	
109	**Retrieval Q.** Name Claude Code's three essential elements and the claim they justify. *(Reasoning model + consistent long tool chains + right agent architecture; reliable agentic coding at scale wasn't possible before it.)*
110	
111	---
112	
113	## Idea 7 — Programmable agentic coding: the agent as a function call
114	
115	**Hook.** The lesson's biggest unlock is almost a throwaway line: Claude Code runs in the terminal. Which means any programming language with terminal access can *call it*. Which means the agent is no longer an app you sit in front of — it's a component you build with.
116	
117	**Picture.** Frame t1063 (17:43): the `programmable/` directory — three launchers + `prompt.md`. Frame t1105 (18:25): `programmable.py` on screen, ~30 lines. Frame t1205 (20:05): the headless run's final REPORT in the terminal. Frame t1000 (16:40): the README-35-lines shot that frames this whole section.
118	
119	**Worked example.** All three launchers are the same five steps in different costumes — read `programmable/prompt.md`, pass it to `claude -p`, capture output, print it, propagate errors:
120	
121	- `programmable.sh` — `PROMPT_CONTENT="$(cat programmable/prompt.md)"; OUTPUT="$(claude -p "$PROMPT_CONTENT")"; echo "$OUTPUT"` (3 lines; the pattern with nothing else)
122	- `programmable.py` — `subprocess.run(["claude", "-p", prompt_content], capture_output=True, text=True)`, print stdout/stderr, `sys.exit(returncode)` (the variant Dan runs; the most production-shaped: error handling + exit-code propagation)
123	- `programmable.ts` — Bun: `await $\`claude -p ${promptContent}\`.text()` then log (proves language choice is irrelevant)
124	
125	`prompt.md` itself is a *superset* of the README demo and self-contained: it creates BOTH `main_aic.py` and `main_tac.py` (no dependency on a prior interactive run), and adds a fourth block the README prompt lacks — `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. That REPORT block is the seed of every report-back/verification pattern in later AI developer workflows: headless runs must *tell you what happened*.
126	
127	Demo order matters and is worth reproducing exactly: delete the branch from the interactive run first (`git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`), then `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` from `main` — and watch the whole workflow re-materialize without you.
128	
129	**Dan's term.** *Programmable agentic coding* / a *programmable agentic coding tool*. Why it matters: "we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle" — across all developer environments, "including full agentic environments where we're not even present," with *agentic triggers* (a later-course topic) deciding when they fire. "It's not just about the agentic prompt. It's about **where** we can use the agentic prompt."
130	
131	**Failure mode.** Watching instead of running — the scripts look too trivial to bother with, so the student never feels the qualitative difference between *chatting with* an agent and *invoking* one. Second failure: missing that `prompt.md` ≠ the README prompt (the superset + REPORT differences are exactly the parts that make headless runs viable). Third: not realizing `.env.sample` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=`) marks the API-billing path that headless/CI usage implies.
132	
133	**Retrieval Q.** What one property of Claude Code makes it programmable, and what does prompt.md's REPORT block demand? *(It runs in the terminal, so any language with terminal access can invoke `claude -p`; REPORT demands the exact output of both .py files.)*
134	
135	---
136	
137	## Idea 8 — The contradicting truth: replace yourself
138	
139	**Hook.** The lesson ends on a paradox sharp enough to be the course's motto: *to become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.* The engineer who automates their own work owns the automation — and no vibe coder will replicate what that engineer can do.
140	
141	**Picture.** t1250 (20:50) is B-roll (hands typing) — render this beat as a designed pull-quote, not a frame (`diagram_instead: true` in the frame plan).
142	
143	**Worked example.** Lesson 1's arc in miniature already performed it: the engineer ran a prompt interactively (doing the work), then scripted the same prompt (`programmable/*`), making themselves unnecessary for that workflow — permanently. Multiply by every workflow you own: that's the course.
144	
145	**Dan's term.** *The contradicting truth.* Supporting frame: evolution — "Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adapt new ones and bet on potential futures. But in the tech industry, this is where all the alpha lies... your asymmetric engineering advantage exists... in the future." Teaser for lesson 2: leverage points such that *10 minutes of your work equals 60+ minutes of another engineer's*.
146	
147	**Failure mode.** Reading the paradox as job-loss fatalism (and disengaging) instead of as the leverage strategy it is. The resolution the student must be able to articulate: what gets replaced is your *typing*; what becomes irreplaceable is your *judgment about what to build and your ownership of the systems that build it*.
148

# TAC-1 · Hello Agentic Coding — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 21:51 · Beginner · Tactic #1: **Stop Coding**
> Lesson artifact: a 35-line README, one settings file, and three ~20-line launcher scripts. That's the whole codebase, on purpose.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** AI coding (generating code from prompts) was phase one; agentic coding — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools inside a programmable agent — is phase two, and the engineer who commands it becomes irreplaceable by replacing themselves.

**The chapter must land eight ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — A new role exists: the Agentic Engineer

**Hook.** In 2023, before it was obvious, Dan bought a domain name as a bet: agenticengineer.com. The bet was that a new software role would emerge, defined not by writing code but by *building systems that can take actions as we can*. Lesson 1 opens by declaring the bet settled: the role now exists, and this course exists to move you into it.

**Picture.** Frame t0078 (1:18): the agenticengineer.com page on screen while Dan narrates the 2023 prediction. Frame t0115 (1:55): the two-phase timeline — Phase 1 "AI CODING" (vibe coders born, code commoditized) flowing into Phase 2 "AGENTIC CODING" (real engineers strike back).

**Worked example.** The entire lesson repo *is* the role in miniature: nothing in `tac/tac-1` is application code. It's a README of prompts, a permissions file, and launchers — artifacts of someone who directs systems rather than types programs.

**Dan's term.** *Phase two Agentic Engineer.* Also the era framing: *"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back."*

**Failure mode.** Hearing "new role" as a title change rather than a job change. The weak student keeps doing phase-1 work (prompt → code → paste) with a new label. The role's actual definition — building systems that take actions — is testable: if nothing runs without you pressing the keys, you're still phase one.

**Retrieval Q.** What defines the agentic engineer role, in Dan's 2023 prediction wording? *(Building systems that can take actions as we can.)*

---

## Idea 2 — The mission: become the engineer they can't replace

**Hook.** "You know who *they* are. It's your boss. It's the company. It's the industry. It's AI." Nothing in tech is forever — and in a world where your grandma or your little brother can build an app with one prompt, what exactly makes *you* hard to replace?

**Picture.** Frame t0124 (2:04): the mission slide. Frame t0162 (2:42): the full-screen **COMMANDER OF COMPUTE** title card — the answer to the question the mission poses.

**Worked example.** The answer performed, not stated: by lesson end, a Python script (`programmable/programmable.py`) does a complete branch-write-run-commit-report cycle while the engineer watches. The engineer's contribution moved up one level: they wrote the prompt and the trigger, not the code.

**Dan's term.** *Commander of compute* — "We do what we always do in technological revolutions. We move up the stack once again." And the strategy: *build systems that build systems*. The economics: the fabled *10x engineer* comes from 10x **leverage**, never 10x time — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find. Also the end-state: codebases as *self-operating machines* that "literally run themselves."

**Failure mode.** Treating the mission as motivational garnish and skipping to the demo. The mission is load-bearing: every later tactic is justified by "does this increase your leverage per unit of attention?" Students who skip it evaluate tactics by comfort instead.

**Retrieval Q.** Who are "they" in "an engineer they can't replace," and what is the one-word strategy for becoming that engineer? *(Boss, company, industry, AI; leverage — commanding compute to build systems that build systems.)*

---

## Idea 3 — Tactic #1: Stop Coding

**Hook.** The first tactic is dead simple, mission critical, and potentially uncomfortable. Dan says it twice for complete clarity: **Stop coding.** Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop. This from a man who spent a decade-plus hand-coding at startups and large companies and admits he misses it.

**Picture.** Frame t0414 (6:54): the Tactic #1 reveal. The chapter's headline image.

**Worked example.** Negative space in the codebase: `tac/tac-1` contains zero hand-written application code, and the course promise is that *throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code gets typed*. `main_aic.py` and `main_tac.py` exist only after an agent creates them.

**Dan's term.** *Stop coding.* The supporting cast: "powerful language models [in] agentic loops running on powerful supercomputers are now vastly superior coders than you and I are"; "you're an engineer, not a coder — the difference is massive"; and the reallocation target — *planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures*.

**Failure mode.** Two opposite misreadings, both fatal. (a) "No more code" — wrong: code is still a primary asset that generates features and products; you'll generate more than ever. (b) "No more understanding code" — wrong: code understanding remains critically important; review is where your cycles go. And the behavioral failure: agreeing in theory, then hand-editing the agent's output at the first imperfection instead of re-prompting — which trains you to distrust the loop and forfeits the tactic entirely.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the two things "stop coding" does NOT mean, and where the freed cycles go. *(Doesn't mean stop generating code or stop understanding it; cycles go to planning, reviewing, closed-loop structures.)*

---

## Idea 4 — Big Three → Core Four: the one-dimension delta

**Hook.** Everything that changed between phase one and phase two is a single added dimension. You already know it — it's been hiding in plain sight, getting more capable over time.

**Picture.** Frame t0845 (14:05): the Core Four Venn diagram — CONTEXT (blue), TOOLS (yellow), MODEL (red), PROMPT (green), overlapping over a dimmed view of the lesson README. The one diagram to memorize from lesson 1.

**Worked example.** `.claude/settings.json` is the "tools" circle made concrete — the exact tool surface the demo runs on: `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, `Bash(git checkout:*)`, `Bash(git branch:*)`, `Bash(git add:*)`, `Bash(git commit:*)`, `WebSearch`. Read it and you can predict everything the agentic prompt is able to do — and everything it isn't.

**Dan's term.** *The big three* (context, model, prompt — "always there even if you can't see it") upgraded by tools to *the core four*. Precise wording matters: the new element is *"prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools."* And the pre-emptive rebuttal to "tool calling isn't new": *"It's not a question of new. It's a question of scale and performance."*

**Failure mode.** Shrugging "big whoop, who cares — prompts call tools now" (Dan names this exact shrug). The weak student files the core four as vocabulary instead of as a diagnostic: when an agentic run goes wrong, the cause is always one of the four — wrong context, wrong model, wrong prompt, or wrong/missing tools. Students who internalize it debug systematically; students who don't just re-roll the prompt.

**Retrieval Q.** What upgrades the big three to the core four — exact phrasing — and what is Dan's answer to "tool calling isn't new"? *(Prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools; it's not a question of new but of scale and performance.)*

---

## Idea 5 — Two prompts, one README: AI coding vs agentic coding

**Hook.** The lesson's centerpiece is an A/B test you run on your own machine. Same repo, same agent, same afternoon — two prompts. One generates a file. The other does engineering. The difference between them, Dan insists, is *monumental*.

**Picture.** Before/after pair: frame t0700 (11:40) — the AI coding prompt creating `main_aic.py`, nothing you haven't seen a million times; frame t0748 (12:28) — Claude Code converting the agentic prompt into a todo checklist; frame t0790 (13:10) — the full trace: `git checkout -b demo-agentic-coding`, `Write(main_tac.py)`, both `uv run` outputs, `git add`, `git commit`, todos checked off.

**Worked example.** From `README.md` (35 lines — Dan's count is exact):

- **AI Coding Prompt:** `CREATE main_aic.py: print goodbye ai coding` → one file, one print. Phase 1: code generation, full stop.
- **Agentic Coding Prompt:** `RUN:` checkout new/existing `demo-agentic-coding` branch → `CREATE main_tac.py:` print "hello agentic coding" + a concise definition of AI agents → `RUN:` `uv run main_aic.py`, `uv run main_tac.py`, `git add .`, `git commit -m "Demo agentic coding capabilities"` → the agent plans, executes step by step, cleans up its todos, reports what it did.

Note the prompt's *shape*: RUN/CREATE/RUN reads like a runbook. The prompt is a workflow specification, and the verbs are tool calls.

**Dan's term.** *The Agentic (Coding) Prompt* — "a prompt contains a sequence of tool calls." And the observation that unlocks it: "Claude Code is not just writing code. It's calling tools. It's doing engineering work."

**Failure mode.** Concluding the prompts are equivalent "because both made files appear." The tell that a student missed the lesson: they can't list what the second prompt did that the first didn't (branch, execute, commit, report). Secondary failure: not rerunning the demo after deleting the branch, so they never see that the workflow is *reproducible* — the property everything in later lessons depends on.

**Retrieval Q.** List everything the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't. *(Branch checkout, second file creation per spec, running both programs, git add + commit, todo management + report.)*

---

## Idea 6 — Why Claude Code: the three essential elements

**Hook.** If prompts could always call tools, why did agentic coding only now become real? Because the tools changed and the models improved — and one tool combined the ingredients properly first. There's a new form factor of engineering to take into account.

**Picture.** Frame t0903 (15:03): the three-elements slide. Frame t0608 (10:08): the humble on-ramp — VS Code, Cmd+J, `claude`, boot screen.

**Worked example.** The demo itself is the evidence: a 12-line prompt produced a plan, five tool executions in the right order with correct recovery of context between them, and a report — with zero baby-sitting. That reliability across a *long chain* is the differentiator the slide names.

**Dan's term.** The *three essential elements*: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed; (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools; (3) the right agent architecture. Result: "Reliable agentic coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code." Positioning: "Just as Aider was for the AI coding phase one era, Claude Code represents the best phase two agentic coding tool" — being copied by every other tool. Economics stated plainly: millions and millions of tokens; have the funds or the plan; *pay to play* for maximum ROI. And the anti-lock-in clause: tactics are *transferable* — "don't get stuck on any one tool."

**Failure mode.** Tool fixation in either direction: (a) treating the lesson as expired because the UI/models changed — Dan pre-handles this on camera ("your Claude Code UI might look different... that's all great"); (b) fanboy-ing the tool and missing that the three elements are a *checklist for evaluating any agentic tool*, which is the transferable part.

**Retrieval Q.** Name Claude Code's three essential elements and the claim they justify. *(Reasoning model + consistent long tool chains + right agent architecture; reliable agentic coding at scale wasn't possible before it.)*

---

## Idea 7 — Programmable agentic coding: the agent as a function call

**Hook.** The lesson's biggest unlock is almost a throwaway line: Claude Code runs in the terminal. Which means any programming language with terminal access can *call it*. Which means the agent is no longer an app you sit in front of — it's a component you build with.

**Picture.** Frame t1063 (17:43): the `programmable/` directory — three launchers + `prompt.md`. Frame t1105 (18:25): `programmable.py` on screen, ~30 lines. Frame t1205 (20:05): the headless run's final REPORT in the terminal. Frame t1000 (16:40): the README-35-lines shot that frames this whole section.

**Worked example.** All three launchers are the same five steps in different costumes — read `programmable/prompt.md`, pass it to `claude -p`, capture output, print it, propagate errors:

- `programmable.sh` — `PROMPT_CONTENT="$(cat programmable/prompt.md)"; OUTPUT="$(claude -p "$PROMPT_CONTENT")"; echo "$OUTPUT"` (3 lines; the pattern with nothing else)
- `programmable.py` — `subprocess.run(["claude", "-p", prompt_content], capture_output=True, text=True)`, print stdout/stderr, `sys.exit(returncode)` (the variant Dan runs; the most production-shaped: error handling + exit-code propagation)
- `programmable.ts` — Bun: `await $\`claude -p ${promptContent}\`.text()` then log (proves language choice is irrelevant)

`prompt.md` itself is a *superset* of the README demo and self-contained: it creates BOTH `main_aic.py` and `main_tac.py` (no dependency on a prior interactive run), and adds a fourth block the README prompt lacks — `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. That REPORT block is the seed of every report-back/verification pattern in later AI developer workflows: headless runs must *tell you what happened*.

Demo order matters and is worth reproducing exactly: delete the branch from the interactive run first (`git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`), then `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` from `main` — and watch the whole workflow re-materialize without you.

**Dan's term.** *Programmable agentic coding* / a *programmable agentic coding tool*. Why it matters: "we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle" — across all developer environments, "including full agentic environments where we're not even present," with *agentic triggers* (a later-course topic) deciding when they fire. "It's not just about the agentic prompt. It's about **where** we can use the agentic prompt."

**Failure mode.** Watching instead of running — the scripts look too trivial to bother with, so the student never feels the qualitative difference between *chatting with* an agent and *invoking* one. Second failure: missing that `prompt.md` ≠ the README prompt (the superset + REPORT differences are exactly the parts that make headless runs viable). Third: not realizing `.env.sample` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=`) marks the API-billing path that headless/CI usage implies.

**Retrieval Q.** What one property of Claude Code makes it programmable, and what does prompt.md's REPORT block demand? *(It runs in the terminal, so any language with terminal access can invoke `claude -p`; REPORT demands the exact output of both .py files.)*

---

## Idea 8 — The contradicting truth: replace yourself

**Hook.** The lesson ends on a paradox sharp enough to be the course's motto: *to become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.* The engineer who automates their own work owns the automation — and no vibe coder will replicate what that engineer can do.

**Picture.** t1250 (20:50) is B-roll (hands typing) — render this beat as a designed pull-quote, not a frame (`diagram_instead: true` in the frame plan).

**Worked example.** Lesson 1's arc in miniature already performed it: the engineer ran a prompt interactively (doing the work), then scripted the same prompt (`programmable/*`), making themselves unnecessary for that workflow — permanently. Multiply by every workflow you own: that's the course.

**Dan's term.** *The contradicting truth.* Supporting frame: evolution — "Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adapt new ones and bet on potential futures. But in the tech industry, this is where all the alpha lies... your asymmetric engineering advantage exists... in the future." Teaser for lesson 2: leverage points such that *10 minutes of your work equals 60+ minutes of another engineer's*.

**Failure mode.** Reading the paradox as job-loss fatalism (and disengaging) instead of as the leverage strategy it is. The resolution the student must be able to articulate: what gets replaced is your *typing*; what becomes irreplaceable is your *judgment about what to build and your ownership of the systems that build it*.

**Retrieval Q.** State the contradicting truth and resolve it in one sentence. *(To become irreplaceable you'll replace yourself — you automate your current work, and the irreplaceable part becomes your command of the systems doing it.)*

---

3	Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
10	AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
11	*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?
12	
13	**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
14	Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
15	*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."
16	
17	**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
18	The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.
19	
20	**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
21	`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery
26	
27	**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
28	Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.
29	
30	**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
31	It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.
32	
33	**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
34	Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.
35	
36	**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
37	(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.
38	
39	**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
40	`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.
41	
42	**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
43	Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going
48	
49	**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
50	Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.
51	
52	**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
53	And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.
54	
55	**13. Pay to play.**
56	Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.
57	
58	**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
59	Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.
60	
61	**15. The mission has named enemies.**
62	"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## Micro-quiz (close the book first)
67	
68	1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
69	2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
70	3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
71	4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
72	5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
73	6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?
74	
75	*(Answers: extract.md ideas 4, 5, 4/6, 7, 7, 8.)*

AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?

**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."

**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.

**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.

**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.

**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.

**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.

**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.

**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.

**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.

**13. Pay to play.**
Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.

**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.

**15. The mission has named enemies.**
"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?

*(Answers: extract.md ideas 4, 5, 4/6, 7, 7, 8.)*

6

8

10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22

24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.

26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33

35

1	# TAC-1 Lab Spec — Hello Agentic Coding
2	
3	**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-1`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git`). No external repos, no extra dependencies beyond the lesson's prerequisite tools.
4	**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Even file edits in the stretch drills go through Claude Code.
5	**Time box:** 45–75 minutes. Token cost: one interactive demo pair + 3–5 headless runs (small; but real — pay to play).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0 · Setup (10 min)
10	
11	1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git && cd tac-1`
12	2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
13	3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
14	   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
15	   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
16	   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
17	4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.
18	
19	**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.
20	
21	## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)
22	
23	**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
24	- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
25	- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.
26	
27	**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
28	- Verify all five engineering actions:
29	  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
30	  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
31	  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
32	  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
33	  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos
34	
35	**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.
36	
37	## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)
38	
39	1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
40	2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
41	3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
42	4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
43	5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
44	   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
45	   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`
46	
47	**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*
48	
49	## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)
50	
51	**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.
52	
53	**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.
54	
55	**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*
56	
57	**S4 — Map to your job (transfer).** Time drill 1A and 1B. Then write two lists from your actual work: tasks that are AI-coding-prompt-shaped vs agentic-coding-prompt-shaped. Circle the one agentic-shaped task you'd automate first with the `programmable/` pattern.
58	
59	## Pass criteria (all required)
60	
61	- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere in the lab
62	- [ ] Permissions audit answers correct (checkpoint 0)
63	- [ ] Five-action delta list correct (checkpoint 1)
64	- [ ] `demo-agentic-coding` branch exists with commit `Demo agentic coding capabilities` containing `main_aic.py` + `main_tac.py`
65	- [ ] `uv run main_tac.py` prints "hello agentic coding" + a one-line AI-agent definition
66	- [ ] All three (or four, with S2) launchers completed headlessly with a REPORT matching the real outputs
67	- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: the core four; the one-dimension delta; Claude Code's three essential elements; the contradicting truth resolved in one sentence
68	
69	## Instructor / self-check notes
70	
71	- **Most common stall:** the "new/existing branch" wording — if the branch already exists from a prior run, the agent may reuse it and the student thinks something broke. Fix: always `git branch -D demo-agentic-coding` between runs (Dan does exactly this on camera at ~17:56).
72	- **Second stall:** running the programmable script from inside the `demo-agentic-coding` branch instead of `main` — teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
73	- **Cost anxiety:** each headless run is a small number of agent turns; the lab total is modest. If a student can't run it at all, the budget conversation (pay to play) is the actual lesson surfacing early.
74	- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** skills, triggers, parallelism, CI embedding — later lessons. Deflect scope creep to keep the primitive crisp.
