1	# Elite Context Engineering
2	
3	> A focused engineer is a performant engineer AND a focused agent is a performant agent.
4	
5	
6	## Purpose
7	
8	- Master the R&D framework to optimize your context windows for high performance agentic coding
9	- Prevent context bloat and context rot through systematic reduction
10	- Delegate effectively to preserve your primary agent's focus
11	- Manage your context window so your model and prompt have the maximum effective context
12	
13	## Setup
14	
15	1. Copy `.env.sample` to `.env`
16	2. Add your API keys:
17	   - `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` - For Claude API access
18	   - `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` - For TTS features
19	   - `OPENAI_API_KEY` - For OpenAI integrations
20	
21	## The R&D Framework
22	
23	*A focused engineer is a performant engineer.*  
24	**A focused agent is a performant agent.**
25	
26	Context engineering is the name of the game for high-value engineering in the age of agents. So, how good are your context engineering skills?
27	
28	There are 3 levels of context engineering techniques and a fourth, **hidden level**, if you're on the bleeding edge pushing into 'Agentic Engineering'.
29	
30	### Why Context Engineering Matters
31	
32	The context window is the PRECIOUS and DELICATE resource that determines your agent's performance. There's a sweet spot - a range of context where your agent performs at maximum capability for the task at hand.
33	
34	There are only two ways to manage your context window effectively:
35	
36	**R and D - Reduce and Delegate**
37	
38	- **Reduce**: Remove junk context, minimize token usage, focus on what matters
39	- **Delegate**: Offload work to sub-agents, separate agents, or specialized systems
40	
41	The real skill in context engineering is **search and destroy** - finding the right context agentically while removing or delegating everything else.
42	
43	## Levels
44	
45	- Beginner
46	- Intermediate
47	- Advanced
48	- Agentic
49	
50	### Technique #1: Measure to Manage
51	
52	> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Foundation for R&D**
53	
54	> What gets measured gets managed. Your agent's context window is a precious, limited resource.
55	
56	The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding. You must measure it to improve it.
57	
58	Two primary tools:
59	- **`/context` Command**: Shows exactly how much context your agent processes EVERY prompt execution
60	- **Token Counters**: Extensions that give real-time estimates BEFORE adding files to context
61	
62	This foundational technique enables everything else. Without actively monitoring your agent's context state, you're just "vibe coding" - limited to low-hanging fruit in a saturated space.
63	
64	To push further, learn to see from your agent's perspective by constantly measuring and managing the context window.
65	
66	### Technique #2: Avoid MCP Servers
67	
68	> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Reduce**
69	
70	> MCP Servers consume your context window on agent startup.
71	>
72	> Often times we don't need the MCP Servers.
73	>
74	> So we should avoid MCP Servers when possible to preserve the context window to prevent context bloat and context rot.
75	
76	There are 3 scopes for MCP servers:
77	
78	- Local scope: `claude mcp {add|remove|list|get|add-json|...}` run `claude mcp --help` for all options
79	- User Scope: `claude mcp ... --scope user ...`
80	- Project scope: `path/to/repo/.mcp.json`
81	
82	Use `claude mcp list` to list all MCP servers.
83	
84	Use `claude --mcp-config .mcp.json --strict-mcp-config` to only include MCP servers that are defined in the `.mcp.json` file.
85	
86	Avoid user and local scope global MCP servers `~/.claude/.mcp.json`. Why? Because you likely don't ALWAYS need them.
87	
88	Instead use no mcp servers to start, then use `claude --mcp-config <some specific mcp.json file>`.
89	
90	If you do still want global MCP servers (user or local scope) and you want to exclusively use a specific MCP server to overwrite the global MCP servers for a single Claude Code instance, you can use `claude --mcp-config <some specific mcp.json file> --strict-mcp-config`. This will override the global MCP servers for that single Claude Code instance and only use the MCP servers defined in the specific mcp.json file.
91	
92	### Technique #3: MORE Prime Less CLAUDE.md
93	
94	> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Reduce**
95	
96	> Context priming over static memory files. Dynamic, controllable setup beats always-on context.
97	
98	The problem with CLAUDE.md (or any auto-loading memory file):
99	- It's always loaded into your agent's context window
100	- Engineering work changes constantly, but the file doesn't
101	- Grows bloated with context not relevant to every task
102	- Risk of contradictory information as teams add content
103	
104	**Solution: Context Priming**
105	
106	Instead of static files, use dedicated custom slash commands to prime your agent for specific task types:
107	- `/prime` - Basic codebase understanding
108	- `/prime_bug` - Bug fixing context
109	- `/prime_feature` - Feature development setup
110	- `/prime_testing` - Testing-specific context
111	
112	Stack commands for specialized workflows: `/prime_cc` executes base prime then loads all .claude files for Claude Code-specific work.
113	
114	Your CLAUDE.md should only contain absolute universals needed 100% of the time. Everything else: prime dynamically.
115	
116	### Technique #4: Control Output Tokens
117	
118	> Level: Intermediate | **Framework: Reduce**
119	
120	> Output tokens cost 3-5x more than input tokens. Control them with output styles.
121	
122	Output tokens are the most expensive part of your agent and get added back to context, creating compound costs.
123	
124	Claude Code's output styles let you limit and guide token generation:
125	- `concise-done.md` - Minimal responses, just "Done."
126	- `concise-ultra.md` - Ultra-brief responses
127	- `verbose-yaml-structured.md` - Structured but detailed
128	
129	Example impact: Simple "What does this codebase do?" prompt

# Elite Context Engineering

> A focused engineer is a performant engineer AND a focused agent is a performant agent.


## Purpose

- Master the R&D framework to optimize your context windows for high performance agentic coding
- Prevent context bloat and context rot through systematic reduction
- Delegate effectively to preserve your primary agent's focus
- Manage your context window so your model and prompt have the maximum effective context

## Setup

1. Copy `.env.sample` to `.env`
2. Add your API keys:
   - `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` - For Claude API access
   - `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` - For TTS features
   - `OPENAI_API_KEY` - For OpenAI integrations

## The R&D Framework

*A focused engineer is a performant engineer.*  
**A focused agent is a performant agent.**

Context engineering is the name of the game for high-value engineering in the age of agents. So, how good are your context engineering skills?

There are 3 levels of context engineering techniques and a fourth, **hidden level**, if you're on the bleeding edge pushing into 'Agentic Engineering'.

### Why Context Engineering Matters

The context window is the PRECIOUS and DELICATE resource that determines your agent's performance. There's a sweet spot - a range of context where your agent performs at maximum capability for the task at hand.

There are only two ways to manage your context window effectively:

**R and D - Reduce and Delegate**

- **Reduce**: Remove junk context, minimize token usage, focus on what matters
- **Delegate**: Offload work to sub-agents, separate agents, or specialized systems

The real skill in context engineering is **search and destroy** - finding the right context agentically while removing or delegating everything else.

## Levels

- Beginner
- Intermediate
- Advanced
- Agentic

### Technique #1: Measure to Manage

> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Foundation for R&D**

> What gets measured gets managed. Your agent's context window is a precious, limited resource.

The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding. You must measure it to improve it.

Two primary tools:
- **`/context` Command**: Shows exactly how much context your agent processes EVERY prompt execution
- **Token Counters**: Extensions that give real-time estimates BEFORE adding files to context

This foundational technique enables everything else. Without actively monitoring your agent's context state, you're just "vibe coding" - limited to low-hanging fruit in a saturated space.

To push further, learn to see from your agent's perspective by constantly measuring and managing the context window.

### Technique #2: Avoid MCP Servers

> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Reduce**

> MCP Servers consume your context window on agent startup.
>
> Often times we don't need the MCP Servers.
>
> So we should avoid MCP Servers when possible to preserve the context window to prevent context bloat and context rot.

There are 3 scopes for MCP servers:

- Local scope: `claude mcp {add|remove|list|get|add-json|...}` run `claude mcp --help` for all options
- User Scope: `claude mcp ... --scope user ...`
- Project scope: `path/to/repo/.mcp.json`

Use `claude mcp list` to list all MCP servers.

Use `claude --mcp-config .mcp.json --strict-mcp-config` to only include MCP servers that are defined in the `.mcp.json` file.

Avoid user and local scope global MCP servers `~/.claude/.mcp.json`. Why? Because you likely don't ALWAYS need them.

Instead use no mcp servers to start, then use `claude --mcp-config <some specific mcp.json file>`.

If you do still want global MCP servers (user or local scope) and you want to exclusively use a specific MCP server to overwrite the global MCP servers for a single Claude Code instance, you can use `claude --mcp-config <some specific mcp.json file> --strict-mcp-config`. This will override the global MCP servers for that single Claude Code instance and only use the MCP servers defined in the specific mcp.json file.

### Technique #3: MORE Prime Less CLAUDE.md

> Level: Beginner | **Framework: Reduce**

> Context priming over static memory files. Dynamic, controllable setup beats always-on context.

The problem with CLAUDE.md (or any auto-loading memory file):
- It's always loaded into your agent's context window
- Engineering work changes constantly, but the file doesn't
- Grows bloated with context not relevant to every task
- Risk of contradictory information as teams add content

**Solution: Context Priming**

Instead of static files, use dedicated custom slash commands to prime your agent for specific task types:
- `/prime` - Basic codebase understanding
- `/prime_bug` - Bug fixing context
- `/prime_feature` - Feature development setup
- `/prime_testing` - Testing-specific context

Stack commands for specialized workflows: `/prime_cc` executes base prime then loads all .claude files for Claude Code-specific work.

Your CLAUDE.md should only contain absolute universals needed 100% of the time. Everything else: prime dynamically.

### Technique #4: Control Output Tokens

> Level: Intermediate | **Framework: Reduce**

> Output tokens cost 3-5x more than input tokens. Control them with output styles.

Output tokens are the most expensive part of your agent and get added back to context, creating compound costs.

Claude Code's output styles let you limit and guide token generation:
- `concise-done.md` - Minimal responses, just "Done."
- `concise-ultra.md` - Ultra-brief responses
- `verbose-yaml-structured.md` - Structured but detailed

Example impact: Simple "What does this codebase do?" prompt
- Default output: ~500 tokens added to context
- Concise style: ~50 tokens added to context

Over tens or hundreds of prompts, this difference compounds massively. A focused agent with controlled output is a performant agent.

### Technique #5: Use Sub Agents - PROPERLY

> Level: Intermediate | **Framework: Delegate**  

> Sub agents create "partially forked context windows" - their system prompts don't consume your primary agent's context.

When you use sub agents correctly:
- System prompts stay isolated from primary context
- Sub agents respond to your primary agent, not you
- Primary agent prompts sub agents based on your instructions

Best for tasks that can operate in isolation with minimal context from primary agent. Example: `/load_ai_docs` delegates documentation fetching to parallel sub agents, protecting primary context.

Key: Write sub agents to return concise, reduced reports to your primary agent. This is delegation at work - the D in the R&D (Reduce & Delegate) framework.

### Technique #6: Use the Architect Editor Multi-Agent Pattern

> Level: Intermediate | **Framework: R&D (Reduce via Delegation)**

> Separate planning from implementation. A focused agent is a performant agent.

Two agents working side by side:
1. **Architect/Planner**: Gathers context, explores options, creates spec files
2. **Editor/Builder**: Reads spec, implements with surgical precision

The planner wastes tokens finding the right context - that's its job. The implementor gets a crystal-clear context window for error-free edits.

Example workflow:
```bash
/quick-plan "create wrapper system for claude code typescript sdk..."
# Planner explores, creates detailed spec
# Fresh builder agent implements from spec
```

This ensures your implementor has maximum focus for perfect execution.

### Technique #7: Avoid compact - reset and prime

> Level: Advanced | **Framework: Reduce**

> `/compact` is a bandaid. Know your context exactly instead of guessing.

The problem with `/compact`:
- You don't know exactly what's retained
- Always loses key information in compression
- Puts agent in decent but unknown state

**Better approach**: Full reset + context prime
- `/clear` to reset completely  
- `/prime` or `/prime_[task]` to reload exact context
- You know precisely what's in the window

This prepares you for out-loop agentic coding where no single agent should exceed 200k tokens. If it does, chop up the task.

### Technique #8: Use Context Bundles

> Level: Advanced | **Framework: Reduce**

> Track and reuse context across sessions with hooks that capture file operations.

Context bundles automatically capture:
- Files read and written per session
- Stored in `agents/context_bundles/<session_id>_<datetime>.jsonl`
- Quickly reload previous session's exact context

Commands:
- `/status` - Get current session ID
- `/load_bundle <bundle_file>` - Reload previous context
- `/prime_bundle` - Custom prime with bundle loading

This technique enables instant context restoration for fresh agents, building on the reset-and-prime pattern. Perfect for long development sessions.

### Technique #9: Use one agent for one purpose

> Level: Advanced | **Framework: R&D**

> A focused agent is a performant agent. Ship one thing at a time.

This summarizes all previous techniques:
- Forces you to define: "What's this agent's single purpose?"
- Plan the pipeline of agents for complex work
- Each agent has maximum focus for its specific task

Workflow:
1. Plan work completely separate from technology
2. Design agent pipeline (AI Developer Workflow)
3. Execute with single-purpose agents

This is the foundation for scaling to AI Developer Workflows - the highest leverage in agentic coding.

### Technique #10: System Prompt

> Level: Agentic | **Framework: Reduce**

> Gain fine-tuned control with `--append-system-prompt` and the SDK's `customSystemPrompt`.

Control Claude Code's behavior at the deepest level:
- `--append-system-prompt` - Add to existing system prompt
- `customSystemPrompt` (SDK) - Complete overwrite (dangerous!)

Example: Force incremental file reading:
```bash
claude --append-system-prompt "ALWAYS read files in 100-line increments..."
```

This trades time for context - agent reads chunks of 100 instead of entire files.

Only use when nothing else works or building custom out-loop agents. The Claude Code team has carefully crafted the default prompt.

### Technique #11: Primary Multi-Agent Delegation

> Level: Agentic | **Framework: Delegate**

> Orchestrate multiple primary agents. Maximum delegation with complete context isolation.

Unlike sub agents, primary agents are completely independent:
- Full Claude Code instances with separate context
- Can use different models, settings, prompts
- Report back via files or structured outputs

Lightweight implementation: `/background` command
```bash
/background "/quick-plan ..." sonnet report.md
```

Agents orchestrating agents - compute managing compute. Perfect for parallel work streams.

Be careful: Runs directly on your API keys. Must be managed properly.

### Technique #12: Agent Experts

> Level: Agentic | **Framework: R&D**

> Self-improving specialized agents with plan-build-improve cycles.

Agent Experts are specialized agent sets for codebase areas:
- **Plan**: Investigate and create specifications
- **Build**: Execute from specifications  
- **Improve**: Update expert knowledge based on work done

Example workflow:
```bash
/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_plan "implement session logging..."
/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_build <path_to_plan>
/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_improve
```

The improve step makes experts self-documenting - they update their own knowledge for future runs.

This pattern scales engineering by encoding expertise in reusable, self-improving agent pipelines.

---

## Claude Code Bash Alias

```bash
alias cld="claude"
alias cldp="claude -p"
alias cldo="claude --model opus"
alias clds="claude --model sonnet"
alias cldys="claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model sonnet"
alias cldy="claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model sonnet"
alias cldyo="claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus"
alias lfg="claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus"
alias cldpy="claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions"
alias cldpyo="claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus"
alias cldr="claude --resume"
```

allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
description: Creates a concise engineering implementation plan based on user requirements and saves it to specs directory
model: claude-opus-4-1-20250805
---

# Purpose

This prompt creates a detailed implementation plan based on the user's requirements provided through the `USER_PROMPT` variable. It analyzes the request, thinks through the implementation approach, and saves a comprehensive specification document to `specs/<name-of-plan>.md` that can be used as a blueprint for actual development work.

## Variables

USER_PROMPT: $ARGUMENTS
PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: `specs/`

## Instructions

- Carefully analyze the user's requirements provided in the USER_PROMPT variable
- Think deeply about the best approach to implement the requested functionality or solve the problem
- Create a concise implementation plan that includes:
  - Clear problem statement and objectives
  - Technical approach and architecture decisions
  - Step-by-step implementation guide
  - Potential challenges and solutions
  - Testing strategy
  - Success criteria
- Generate a descriptive, kebab-case filename based on the main topic of the plan
- Save the complete implementation plan to `PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY/<descriptive-name>.md`
- Ensure the plan is detailed enough that another developer could follow it to implement the solution
- Include code examples or pseudo-code where appropriate to clarify complex concepts
- Consider edge cases, error handling, and scalability concerns
- Structure the document with clear sections and proper markdown formatting

## Report

After creating and saving the implementation plan, provide a concise report with the following format:

```
✅ Implementation Plan Created

File: PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY/<filename>.md
Topic: <brief description of what the plan covers>
Key Components:
- <main component 1>
- <main component 2>
- <main component 3>
```

7	# Background Claude Code
8	
9	Run a Claude Code instance in the background to perform tasks autonomously while you continue working.
10	
11	## Variables
12	
13	USER_PROMPT: $1
14	MODEL: $2 (defaults to 'sonnet' if not provided)
15	REPORT_FILE: $3 (defaults to './agents/background/background-report-DAY-NAME_HH_MM_SS.md' if not provided)
16	
17	## Instructions
18	
19	- Capture timestamp in a variable FIRST to ensure consistency across file creation and references
20	- Create the initial report file with header BEFORE launching the background agent
21	- Fire off a new Claude Code instance using the Bash tool with run_in_background=true
22	- IMPORTANT: Pass the `USER_PROMPT` exactly as provided with no modifications
23	- Set the model to either 'sonnet' or 'opus' based on `MODEL` parameter
24	- Configure Claude Code with all necessary flags for automated operation
25	- All report format instructions are embedded in the --append-system-prompt
26	- Use --print flag to run in non-interactive mode
27	- Use --output-format text for standard text output
28	- Use --dangerously-skip-permissions to bypass permission prompts for automated operation
29	- Use all provided cli flags AS IS. Do not alter them.
30	- The append-system-prompt contains all report structure requirements and renaming logic
31	- IMPORTANT: Do not alter the append-system-prompt in anyway.
32	
33	## Workflow
34	
35	1. Create the report directory if it doesn't exist:
36	   ```bash
37	   mkdir -p agents/background
38	   ```
39	
40	2. Set default values for parameters:
41	   - `MODEL`
42	   - `TIMESTAMP` (capture once for consistency)
43	   - `REPORT_FILE` (using the captured timestamp)
44	
45	3. Create the initial report file with just the header (IMPORTANT: Only IF no report file is provided - if it is provided, echo it and skip this step):
46	   Get this into your context window so you know what to pass into the Claude Code command.
47	   ```bash
48	   TIMESTAMP=$(date +%a_%H_%M_%S)
49	   echo "TIMESTAMP: ${TIMESTAMP}"

# Background Claude Code

Run a Claude Code instance in the background to perform tasks autonomously while you continue working.

## Variables

USER_PROMPT: $1
MODEL: $2 (defaults to 'sonnet' if not provided)
REPORT_FILE: $3 (defaults to './agents/background/background-report-DAY-NAME_HH_MM_SS.md' if not provided)

## Instructions

- Capture timestamp in a variable FIRST to ensure consistency across file creation and references
- Create the initial report file with header BEFORE launching the background agent
- Fire off a new Claude Code instance using the Bash tool with run_in_background=true
- IMPORTANT: Pass the `USER_PROMPT` exactly as provided with no modifications
- Set the model to either 'sonnet' or 'opus' based on `MODEL` parameter
- Configure Claude Code with all necessary flags for automated operation
- All report format instructions are embedded in the --append-system-prompt
- Use --print flag to run in non-interactive mode
- Use --output-format text for standard text output
- Use --dangerously-skip-permissions to bypass permission prompts for automated operation
- Use all provided cli flags AS IS. Do not alter them.
- The append-system-prompt contains all report structure requirements and renaming logic
- IMPORTANT: Do not alter the append-system-prompt in anyway.

## Workflow

1. Create the report directory if it doesn't exist:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p agents/background
   ```

2. Set default values for parameters:
   - `MODEL`
   - `TIMESTAMP` (capture once for consistency)
   - `REPORT_FILE` (using the captured timestamp)

3. Create the initial report file with just the header (IMPORTANT: Only IF no report file is provided - if it is provided, echo it and skip this step):
   Get this into your context window so you know what to pass into the Claude Code command.
   ```bash
   TIMESTAMP=$(date +%a_%H_%M_%S)
   echo "TIMESTAMP: ${TIMESTAMP}"
   REPORT_FILE="${REPORT_FILE:-./agents/background/background-report-${TIMESTAMP}.md}"
   echo "REPORT_FILE: ${REPORT_FILE}"
   echo "# Background Agent Report - ${TIMESTAMP}" > "${REPORT_FILE}"
   ```

<primary-agent-delegation>
4. Construct the Claude Code command with all settings:

   - Execute the command using Bash with run_in_background=true

   ```bash
   claude \
     --model "${MODEL}" \
     --output-format text \
     --dangerously-skip-permissions \
     --append-system-prompt "IMPORTANT: You are running as a background agent. Your primary responsibility is to execute work and document your progress continuously in ${REPORT_FILE}. Iteratively write to the report file continuously as you work. Every few tool calls you should update the REPORT_FILE ## Progress section. Follow this file structure.

## CRITICAL WORKFLOW STRUCTURE

   IMPORTANT: You MUST follow this workflow as you work:

   1. The file ${REPORT_FILE} has been created with a header. You must UPDATE as you proceed it (not recreate it) with this EXACT markdown structure:

   ```markdown
   # Background Agent Report - DAY-NAME_HH_MM_SS

   ## Task Understanding
   Clearly state what the user requested. Break down complex requests into numbered items:
   User requested:
   1. [First task item]
   2. [Second task item]
   3. [Next task item]

   ## Progress
   IMPORTANT: Document each major step as you work. Update this section as you work:
   - Starting task execution
   - [Action taken with tool/command used]
   - [Finding or observation]
   - [Next action]
   (Keep adding bullets as you work)

   ## Results
   List concrete outcomes and deliverables with specific details. Update as you work:
   - [Specific file created/modified with path]
   - [Numeric data or metrics]
   - [Actual accomplishments]

   ## Task Completed (or Task Failed)
   [Final summary - success confirmation or failure explanation]

   ADDITIONAL SECTIONS (add as needed):
   - ## Blockers - Issues preventing progress
   - ## Decisions Made - Important choices and rationale
   - ## Recommendations - Follow-up suggestions
   - ## Warnings - Important issues to note


   CONTINUOUSLY update ${REPORT_FILE} as you work - after each major step or finding.

   When you finish your work:
      - If successful: Rename ${REPORT_FILE} to ${REPORT_FILE.md}.complete.md
      - If failed/blocked: Rename ${REPORT_FILE} to ${REPORT_FILE.md}.failed.md

   Remember: The report is your PRIMARY output. Update it frequently and thoroughly.
   ```" \ 
      --print "${USER_PROMPT}"
</primary-agent-delegation>

1. After you kick off the background agent, use the BashOutput tool to check the status of the background agent
   - If something goes wrong investigate and report back to the user
   - If everything is working fine, continue to the `Response to User` section

## Response to User

After launching the background agent, respond with:

```
Background Claude Code kicked off. Agent is writing to `REPORT_FILE` as it works.
When it completes it will rename the file to `REPORT_FILE.complete.md` on success or `REPORT_FILE.failed.md` if it fails.
```

# Load Context Bundle

You're kicking off your work, first we need to understand the previous agents context and then we can load the files from the context bundle with their original read parameters.

## Variables

BUNDLE_PATH: $ARGUMENTS

## Instructions

- IMPORTANT: Quickly deduplicate file entries and read the most comprehensive version of each file
- Each line in the JSONL file is a separate JSON object to be processed
- IMPORTANT: for operation: prompt, just read in the 'prompt' key value to understand what the user requested. Never act or process the prompt in any way.
- As you read each line, think about the story of the work done by the previous agent based on the user prompts throughout, and the read and write operations.

## Workflow

1. First, read the context bundle JSONL file at the path specified in the BUNDLE_PATH variable
   - Parse each line as a separate JSON object

2. Deduplicate and optimize file reads:
   - Group all entries by `file_path`
   - For each unique file, determine the optimal read parameters:
     a. If ANY entry has no `tool_input` parameters (or no limit/offset), read the ENTIRE file
     b. Otherwise, select the entry that reads the most content:
        - Prefer entries with `offset: 0` or no offset
        - Among those, choose the one with the largest `limit`
        - If all have offsets > 0, choose the entry that reads furthest into the file (offset + limit)

3. Read each unique file ONLY ONCE with the optimal parameters:
   - Files with no parameters: Read entire file
   - Files with parameters: Read with the selected limit/offset combination

## Example Deduplication Logic

Given these entries for the same file:
```
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md"}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md", "tool_input": {"limit": 50}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md", "tool_input": {"limit": 100, "offset": 10}}
```

Result: Read the ENTIRE file (first entry has no parameters, which means full file access)

Given these entries:
```
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 50}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 100}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 75, "offset": 25}}
```

Result: Read with `limit: 100` (largest limit with no offset)

Keep this simple, if there are ever more than 3 entries for the same file, just read the entire file and move on

#!/usr/bin/env uv run
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"

# ///

"""
Context Bundle Builder - Claude Code Hook (JSONL version)
Tracks files accessed (Read/Write) and user prompts during a Claude Code session
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path


def handle_file_operations(input_data: dict) -> None:
    """Handle Read/Write tool operations."""
    # Extract relevant data
    session_id = input_data.get("session_id", "unknown")
    tool_name = input_data.get("tool_name", "")
    tool_input = input_data.get("tool_input", {})
    tool_response = input_data.get("tool_response", {})
    
    # Only process Read and Write tools
    if tool_name not in ["Read", "Write"]:
        sys.exit(0)
    
    # Extract file path
    file_path = tool_input.get("file_path")
    if not file_path:
        sys.exit(0)
    
    # Check if Write operation was successful
    if tool_name == "Write" and tool_response:
        success = tool_response.get("success", True)
        if not success:
            sys.exit(0)
    
    # Convert absolute path to relative
    try:
        # Use CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR if available, otherwise use cwd
        project_dir = os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR", os.getcwd())
        abs_path = Path(file_path).resolve()
        project_path = Path(project_dir).resolve()
        
        # Try to make path relative to project directory
        try:
            relative_path = abs_path.relative_to(project_path)
            file_path_relative = str(relative_path)
        except ValueError:
            # If file is outside project directory, keep absolute path
            file_path_relative = file_path
    except Exception:
        # If any error, keep original path
        file_path_relative = file_path
    
    # Create the log entry
    log_entry = {
        "operation": tool_name.lower(),  # "read" or "write"
        "file_path": file_path_relative
    }
    
    # Add tool_input parameters (excluding file_path since we already have it)
    tool_input_filtered = {}
    if tool_name == "Read":
        if "limit" in tool_input:
            tool_input_filtered["limit"] = tool_input["limit"]
        if "offset" in tool_input:
            tool_input_filtered["offset"] = tool_input["offset"]
    elif tool_name == "Write":
        # For Write, we might want to track content length but not the content itself
        if "content" in tool_input:
            tool_input_filtered["content_length"] = len(tool_input.get("content", ""))
    
    # Only add tool_input if there are parameters to save
    if tool_input_filtered:
        log_entry["tool_input"] = tool_input_filtered
    
    # Write to JSONL file
    write_log_entry(session_id, log_entry)


def handle_user_prompt(input_data: dict) -> None:
    """Handle UserPromptSubmit events."""
    # Extract relevant data
    session_id = input_data.get("session_id", "unknown")
    prompt = input_data.get("prompt", "")
    
    if not prompt:
        sys.exit(0)
    
    # Create minimal log entry for prompt
    log_entry = {
        "operation": "prompt",
        "prompt": prompt[:500]  # Limit prompt length to avoid huge logs
    }
    
    # Write to JSONL file
    write_log_entry(session_id, log_entry)


def write_log_entry(session_id: str, log_entry: dict) -> None:
    """Write a log entry to the JSONL file."""
    # Generate filename with day_hour and session_id
    now = datetime.now()
    day_hour = now.strftime("%a_%H").upper()
    
    # Create directory structure
    bundle_dir = Path("agents/context_bundles")
    bundle_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    
    # Use JSONL file (JSON Lines format)
    bundle_file = bundle_dir / f"{day_hour}_{session_id}.jsonl"
    
    # Append to JSONL file (atomic operation for small writes)
    try:
        with open(bundle_file, 'a') as f:
            # Write as a single line of JSON
            f.write(json.dumps(log_entry) + '\n')
    except IOError as e:
        print(f"Error appending to context bundle: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)


def main():
    # Parse command line arguments
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Context Bundle Builder")
    parser.add_argument("--type", choices=["file_ops", "user_prompt"], 
                       default="file_ops",
                       help="Type of operation to handle")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    try:
        # Read hook input from stdin
        input_data = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        print(f"Error parsing JSON input: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    
    # Route to appropriate handler
    if args.type == "file_ops":
        handle_file_operations(input_data)
    elif args.type == "user_prompt":
        handle_user_prompt(input_data)
    
    # Success - exit silently
    sys.exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def create_log_entry(input_data: dict) -> dict:

    return {
        "timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat(),
        "payload": input_data

def write_log_entry(session_id: str, hook_name: str, log_entry: dict) -> None:

    # Append to JSONL file
    with open(log_file, 'a') as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(log_entry) + '\n')


def main():

5. **Verify completeness** - Ensure that the entire documentation content has been captured and saved, not just a summary or excerpt.

**Best Practices:**
- Preserve the original structure and formatting of the documentation
- Maintain all code examples, tables, and important formatting
- Remove only redundant navigation elements and website chrome
- Use descriptive filenames that reflect the content
- Ensure the markdown is properly formatted and readable

Provide your final response in this exact format:
- Success or Failure: `<✅ success>` or `<❌ failure>`
- Markdown file path: `<path_to_saved_file>`

        h,mm,s,ms = int(m.group(1)),int(m.group(2)),int(m.group(3)),int(m.group(4))

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "A focused engineer is a performant engineer AND a focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "0:16", "source": "README + transcript (repeated as the lesson's refrain)" },
    { "text": "Your agent's context window is a precious, renewable, but limited temporal resource.", "approx_timestamp": "3:12" },
    { "text": "The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding.", "approx_timestamp": "3:33" },
    { "text": "Search and destroy is the real skill in context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "2:41" },
    { "text": "When you boil it down, there are only two ways to manage your context window, R and D. Reduce and delegate.", "approx_timestamp": "2:55" },
    { "text": "What gets measured gets managed. So measure your context window.", "approx_timestamp": "5:25" },
    { "text": "If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding, and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "5:13" },
    { "text": "Do not load MCP servers unless you need them... it's very likely you're wasting tokens with MCP servers you're not actively using.", "approx_timestamp": "5:50" },
    { "text": "The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason.", "approx_timestamp": "13:35" },
    { "text": "So prime, don't default. Your CLAUDE.md file should be shrunk to contain only the absolute universal essentials that you're 100% sure you want loaded 100% of the time.", "approx_timestamp": "14:55" },
    { "text": "Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens.", "approx_timestamp": "16:37" },
    { "text": "When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window.", "approx_timestamp": "22:55" },
    { "text": "There's only two ways to manage your context window: reduce context entering your primary agent, and delegate context to sub-agents and to other primary agents.", "approx_timestamp": "26:20" },
    { "text": "By the end of your planning phase, you should be deleting information that isn't relevant to the work you want done. You should go overboard, then delete.", "approx_timestamp": "32:10" },
    { "text": "When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing. I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime.", "approx_timestamp": "34:14" },
    { "text": "You don't want to delegate the control of your context window. You want to own this, just like you want to control your prompt or your model.", "approx_timestamp": "36:00" },
    { "text": "Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused. A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "42:50" },
    { "text": "The system prompt really lets you start controlling how your agent behaves, and when you control the behavior, you control the context window.", "approx_timestamp": "45:40" },
    { "text": "We are kicking off a Claude Code instance from Claude Code. We have compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents. This is where everything is headed. Better agents, and then more agents.", "approx_timestamp": "52:10" },
    { "text": "You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge. This is the agent experts technique.", "approx_timestamp": "57:34" },
    { "text": "It's not necessarily about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly. We manage our context window so that we don't waste time and tokens correcting our agents' mistakes.", "approx_timestamp": "68:38" },
    { "text": "It's a safe bet to bet on context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "70:00" },

    { "text": "A focused engineer is a performant engineer AND a focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "0:16", "source": "README + transcript (repeated as the lesson's refrain)" },

    { "text": "Search and destroy is the real skill in context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "2:41" },
    { "text": "When you boil it down, there are only two ways to manage your context window, R and D. Reduce and delegate.", "approx_timestamp": "2:55" },
    { "text": "What gets measured gets managed. So measure your context window.", "approx_timestamp": "5:25" },
    { "text": "If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding, and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "5:13" },
    { "text": "Do not load MCP servers unless you need them... it's very likely you're wasting tokens with MCP servers you're not actively using.", "approx_timestamp": "5:50" },
    { "text": "The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason.", "approx_timestamp": "13:35" },
    { "text": "So prime, don't default. Your CLAUDE.md file should be shrunk to contain only the absolute universal essentials that you're 100% sure you want loaded 100% of the time.", "approx_timestamp": "14:55" },
    { "text": "Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens.", "approx_timestamp": "16:37" },
    { "text": "When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window.", "approx_timestamp": "22:55" },
    { "text": "There's only two ways to manage your context window: reduce context entering your primary agent, and delegate context to sub-agents and to other primary agents.", "approx_timestamp": "26:20" },
    { "text": "By the end of your planning phase, you should be deleting information that isn't relevant to the work you want done. You should go overboard, then delete.", "approx_timestamp": "32:10" },
    { "text": "When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing. I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime.", "approx_timestamp": "34:14" },
    { "text": "You don't want to delegate the control of your context window. You want to own this, just like you want to control your prompt or your model.", "approx_timestamp": "36:00" },
    { "text": "Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused. A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "42:50" },
    { "text": "The system prompt really lets you start controlling how your agent behaves, and when you control the behavior, you control the context window.", "approx_timestamp": "45:40" },
    { "text": "We are kicking off a Claude Code instance from Claude Code. We have compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents. This is where everything is headed. Better agents, and then more agents.", "approx_timestamp": "52:10" },
    { "text": "You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge. This is the agent experts technique.", "approx_timestamp": "57:34" },
    { "text": "It's not necessarily about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly. We manage our context window so that we don't waste time and tokens correcting our agents' mistakes.", "approx_timestamp": "68:38" },

# AH-1 · Elite Context Engineering — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 73:20 · Lesson #9 · Intermediate · Framework: **R&D — Reduce & Delegate**
> Lesson artifact: a 301-line README that enumerates 12 techniques across 4 levels, plus a full `.claude/` agentic layer (commands, sub-agents, hooks, output styles, an expert triad) and a two-app `apps/` playground. The whole codebase is a context-engineering exhibit.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** A focused agent is a performant agent, and there are only two ways to keep an agent focused — **Reduce** context out of your primary agent and **Delegate** context onto other agents — so master the 12 R&D techniques and you can measure, own, and scale your agents' most precious resource: the context window.

**The chapter must land the framework + 12 techniques + the future.** The framework and each technique below follow: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q. Techniques are grouped by their four levels. Two beats (Technique 9 and the future recap) are rendered as diagrams, not frames.

---

## Idea 0 — The frame: a focused agent is a performant agent (R&D)

**Hook.** You've been told models are getting smarter. True — and irrelevant if you keep drowning them. The bottleneck on a modern agent isn't intelligence; it's the state you cram into its context window. "How good are your context engineering skills? Do you have a skill issue? Let's find out and fix it."

**Picture.** Frame t0176 (2:56): the full-screen **REDUCE AND DELEGATE** title card. Frame t0266 (4:26) is the counter-image: a `/context` readout already at 63k/200k (31%) on boot, with MCP at 24.1k and a bloated memory file at 23.7k — the mess R&D exists to clean up.

**Worked example.** The entire `elite-context-engineering` repo is the framework in miniature: the README lists all 12 techniques tagged by Level (Beginner→Agentic) and Framework (Reduce/Delegate/R&D); the `.claude/` tree is the machinery (priming commands, sub-agents, hooks, output styles, an expert triad). Nothing here is application code for its own sake — it's context-engineering apparatus.

**Dan's term.** *The R&D framework — Reduce and Delegate.* Also: *a focused agent is a performant agent*, *context sweet spot*, *search and destroy*, *core four bullseye*, *context rot / context bloat*.

**Failure mode.** Hearing "context engineering" as "write a good prompt and dump in some files." The weak student never measures, never adopts the agent's perspective, and treats the window as free background plumbing — then blames the model when a bloated window underperforms.

**Retrieval Q.** What are the only two ways to manage a context window, and what's the one-line law behind them? *(Reduce and Delegate; a focused agent is a performant agent.)*

---

# LEVEL 1 — BEGINNER

## Idea 1 — Technique #1: Measure to Manage

**Hook.** You cannot manage what you cannot see. Boot a fresh Claude Code and you might already be a third full — and you'd never know it.

**Picture.** Frame t0266 (4:26): `/context` shows `claude-opus-4-1-20250805 · 63k/200k tokens (31%)`, broken down (System prompt 3.1k, System tools 11.7k, MCP tools 24.1k, Custom agents 122, Memory files 23.7k, Free 137.3k), with the IDE token counter reading `Tokens: 2650` for the README.

**Worked example.** Run `claude`, then `/context`. Install a tokenizer in your IDE so the README's ~2,650 tokens are visible *before* an agent reads it (the README is a high-touch file). Every later technique depends on this one number: how full is the window, and with what?

**Dan's term.** *"What gets measured gets managed. So measure your context window."* Tools: `/context` (what's in the window) and a token counter (what you're about to add).

**Failure mode.** Never running `/context` — "vibe coding," in Dan's words. You optimize a prompt while sitting in a 31%-full, MCP-and-memory-bloated window and can't understand why results wander.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the two measurement tools and what each tells you. *(/context = exact breakdown already in the window; a token counter = a file's cost before it enters context.)*

---

## Idea 2 — Technique #2: Avoid MCP Servers (when you don't need them)

**Hook.** The most expensive thing in your window might be tools you never call.

**Picture.** In t0266, MCP tools = 24.1k (12.1%). Frame t0505 (8:25) is the fix: after `--mcp-config` with firecrawl only, MCP drops to 6.5k (3.2%); the file tree shows the `.mcp.json.*` options.

**Worked example.** Delete the default project `.mcp.json`; avoid global (user/local) servers. Start with none, then load exactly what you need: `claude --mcp-config .mcp.json.firecrawl_7k.sample` (add `--strict-mcp-config` to override globals for that one instance). The repo ships pre-scoped configs and self-fixes the token cost in the filename so you know it up front.

**Dan's term.** *"Do not load MCP servers unless you need them."* The math: ~24k wasted per agent × five agents/hour ≈ 25% of a whole window gone.

**Failure mode.** Keeping a default `.mcp.json` "just in case," silently paying 10–12% of every agent's window for tools you don't use this session.

**Retrieval Q.** How do you load only the MCP server you need, and what flag overrides global servers? *(`claude --mcp-config <file>`; `--strict-mcp-config`.)*

---

## Idea 3 — Technique #3: More Prime, Less CLAUDE.md

**Hook.** The convenience of an always-loaded memory file is exactly what rots your window.

**Picture.** t0266 shows the `⚠ Large CLAUDE.md will impact performance (79.7k chars > 40.0k)` warning with memory files at 23.7k (11.8%). Frame t0786 (13:06): after swapping to the 43-line concise `CLAUDE.md`, memory files fall to 358 tokens (0.2%) and free space is 92.4%.

**Worked example.** `CLAUDE.large.md` (2,978 lines; header literally reads "an example of a BLOATED CLAUDE.md file... the anti-pattern of over-contextualization") vs the 43-line `CLAUDE.md`/`CLAUDE.concise.md`. Instead of a growing memory file, **prime**: `/prime` runs `git ls-files`, reads the README, reports; `/prime_cc` stacks on top to load the `.claude/` layer. Different task → different prime, so the window is always task-scoped.

**Dan's term.** *"The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason."* And: *"Prime, don't default."*

**Failure mode.** Letting CLAUDE.md grow forever into a contradictory 3,000-line glob, and reading the performance warning as noise. Contradictory context is the worst case — it actively steers the agent wrong.

**Retrieval Q.** Why is CLAUDE.md "incredible and terrible for the same reason," and what replaces it? *(It's always loaded; great for guaranteed universals, terrible because it only grows toward irrelevance/contradiction. Replace with context priming + a tiny universals-only CLAUDE.md.)*

---

# LEVEL 2 — INTERMEDIATE

## Idea 4 — Technique #4: Control Output Tokens

**Hook.** Your most expensive tokens are the ones the agent talks back to you with — and they re-enter the window.

**Picture.** Frame t1085 (18:05): left terminal `> hi` → `● Done.`; right terminal the `/output-style` menu (Default, Explanatory, Learning, Ultra Concise, One Word Output, TTS Summary, Bullet Points, YAML Structured).

**Worked example.** Output tokens cost ~3–5× input tokens. You can't cut the tokens spent *writing files*, but you can cut the *response*. The `concise-done.md` "One Word Output" style turns a ~150-token status reply into a 2-token "Done." (~99% off). Output styles hot-swap the output-style block in Claude Code's system prompt. Exceptions: questions and errors still get concise real answers.

**Dan's term.** *"Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens... a massive 99% reduction."* Note the trend teaser: *hot-swapping the system-prompt block.*

**Failure mode.** Dismissing this as trivial at one-agent scale and missing the compounding: 150 vs 2 tokens across hundreds of prompts and agents is a large, recurring drain on your most expensive tokens.

**Retrieval Q.** Why do output styles matter and roughly what was the effect shown? *(Output tokens cost 3–5×; a one-word style cut a ~150-token reply to 2 tokens, ~99%, by hot-swapping the output-style block.)*

---

## Idea 5 — Technique #5: Use Sub-Agents — Properly

**Hook.** What if you could run a big, token-hungry job and have almost none of it touch your main agent?

**Picture.** Frame t1492 (24:52): `load_ai_docs.md` (allowed-tools `Task`, firecrawl) above a terminal reading "Found 10 files... Launching docs-scraper agents…". In `/context`, Custom agents = 122 tokens (0.1%).

**Worked example.** A sub-agent's definition is a **system** prompt, so custom agents cost ~122 tokens in your primary window even though the sub-agent burns thousands doing work. `/load_ai_docs` reads `ai_docs/README.md`, deletes stale docs, and fires `docs-scraper` sub-agents in parallel via the `Task` tool — each scrape (~3k tokens) stays *off* your primary window and returns a concise report to your *primary agent* (not to you).

**Dan's term.** *"When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window."* This is the D — delegation.

**Failure mode.** Spawning sub-agents before you can track one agent's context; losing the flow of information (who prompts whom, who reports to whom). "If you're losing track of a single agent, you probably aren't ready for sub-agents."

**Retrieval Q.** Why do custom sub-agents cost only ~122 tokens in the primary window? *(They're system prompts, not user prompts, so they aren't added to the primary window; the sub-agent burns its own window and reports back to the primary agent.)*

---

## Idea 6 — Technique #6: Architect / Editor (Planner / Builder)

**Hook.** Your best code comes from an agent that never had to *find* anything — it was handed a perfect plan.

**Picture.** Frame t1790 (29:50): split screen — LEFT the planner thinking through the 3-file wrapper spec ("1. A types file... 2. A low-level file that wraps the SDK... 3. A CLI file"), RIGHT a fresh agent at `/clear` then `/build`.

**Worked example.** `/quick-plan` (the architect; `allowed-tools` Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep; writes `specs/<name>.md`) over-gathers context — *that's its job* — then a separate `/build` agent reads only the spec and implements with a clean window. The demo builds `apps/cc_ts_wrapper` (types.ts, core.ts, cli.ts), a Claude Code TypeScript SDK wrapper, from the plan. "You go overboard planning, then delete."

**Dan's term.** *Architect and editor / planner and builder.* Shout-out to legacy AI-coding tools (Aider) that separated planning from building.

**Failure mode.** Prompt-chaining inside one chat window instead of splitting responsibilities, causing context rot with every non-focused prompt and denying the builder a clean window for surgical edits.

**Retrieval Q.** In the architect/editor split, whose job is it to "waste" tokens, and why? *(The planner's — it over-gathers to write a complete spec; you then delete the irrelevant parts so the builder gets a focused window.)*

---

# LEVEL 3 — ADVANCED

## Idea 7 — Technique #7: Avoid /compact — Reset and Prime

**Hook.** After `/compact`, quick — what's in your window right now? You don't know. Neither does Dan.

**Picture.** Frame t2050 (34:10): the builder's finished `cc_ts_wrapper` report (types.ts/core.ts/cli.ts + "Git diff stats: 1 file changed") followed by `> /compact` → "Compacting conversation…".

**Worked example.** `/compact` is a bandaid: it summarizes and leaves an *unknown* state you must Ctrl-R to reread. Instead, `/clear` (blow the window away completely) then `/prime` (reload exactly what you want). You trade a little work for certainty — and it prepares you for out-loop coding, where no single agent should overflow 200k and trigger a compaction you can't predict. If it would, chop up the task.

**Dan's term.** *"When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing... I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime."* And: *"You don't want to delegate the control of your context window."*

**Failure mode.** Reaching for `/compact` reflexively and never knowing the exact window — fine in-loop, fatal the moment you try to scale out-of-loop where predictability is everything.

**Retrieval Q.** Why does Dan avoid `/compact`, and what does he do instead? *(You don't know exactly what's retained; `/clear` then `/prime` so you own and know your exact state.)*

---

## Idea 8 — Technique #8: Use Context Bundles

**Hook.** When an agent's window finally explodes, you don't have to start from zero — you can hand its replacement the story so far.

**Picture.** Frame t2345 (39:05): the `agents/context_bundles/` directory full of `SAT_<hour>_<session>.jsonl` files; one open shows `{"operation":"prompt","prompt":"/prime_cc"}`, `{"operation":"read","file_path":".claude/settings.json"}`, ...; the terminal replays deduped reads.

**Worked example.** A `PostToolUse` hook (`context_bundle_builder.py`) writes an append-only JSONL log of prompts/reads (with limit/offset)/writes to `agents/context_bundles/<DAY_HOUR>_<session_id>.jsonl`. A fresh agent runs `/load_bundle <path>`, which dedups reads (full file if any entry lacks a limit) and replays ~60–70% of the prior agent's state and story — without every detail. Use it selectively.

**Dan's term.** *Context bundle* — *"a simple append-only log of the work that our Claude Code instances are doing... this gets us 70% of where the previous agent was."*

**Failure mode.** Logging every operation and reloading the whole thing — which just overflows the next agent. The trimmed, deduped replay is the point.

**Retrieval Q.** What produces a context bundle and what reloads it? *(A Claude Code hook, `context_bundle_builder.py`, writes per-session JSONL; `/load_bundle` dedups and replays it.)*

---

## Idea 9 — Technique #9: Use One Agent for One Purpose  *(render as diagram)*

**Hook.** The simplest, most powerful rule, and the one that turns techniques into a system: ship one thing at a time.

**Picture.** No unique UI — render as a designed **agent-pipeline (ADW) diagram**: a high-level prompt fanning into single-purpose agents (plan → build → improve → commit).

**Worked example.** It summarizes everything before it. Two-step problem solving: (1) plan the work with *no regard for technology* (users/customers first), then (2) plan how to delegate it across single-purpose agents — an agentic pipeline / AI Developer Workflow (the highest leverage in agentic coding, and the key idea of TAC Lesson 6).

**Dan's term.** *"Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused."* The pipeline is the *ADW*.

**Failure mode.** Making one capable agent own a whole feature; its window rots and you can't tell which part failed. Single-purpose agents localize both focus and debugging.

**Retrieval Q.** What two planning steps does "one agent, one purpose" force? *(Plan the work without regard for technology; then plan the agent pipeline / ADW to deliver it.)*

---

# LEVEL 4 — AGENTIC (the hidden level)

> "Many engineers will not get to this level. Many engineers don't need this level." Here your patterns scale into your ADWs — powerful and dangerous.

## Idea 10 — Technique #10: Modify the System Prompt

**Hook.** Beneath output styles is the real control surface: the system prompt itself.

**Picture.** Frame t2705 (45:05): one command line — `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model sonnet --append-system-prompt "IMPORTANT: When using the Read tool, ALWAYS read in increments of 100 lines... prefix your last message with ✅ or ❌..." -p "what is CLAUDE.large.md for?"`.

**Worked example.** Two knobs: `--append-system-prompt` (adds to Claude Code's crafted default) and the SDK's `customSystemPrompt` (a full *overwrite* — dangerous). Appending must run in **print mode** (`-p`, out-loop). The demo forces the read tool into 100-line increments and a ✅/❌ final-message prefix; the run's context bundle proves obedience — `Read(100)`, `Read(100)` — reducing lines read (and tokens). Points to the Claude Code SDK Mastery extended lesson.

**Dan's term.** *"When you control the behavior, you control the context window."* And the warning: *"Do not use [customSystemPrompt] unless you know what you're doing."*

**Failure mode.** Grabbing `customSystemPrompt` and blowing away the carefully crafted default system prompt. Use `--append-system-prompt` unless you truly need a replacement.

**Retrieval Q.** Which flag appends to the system prompt, what mode is required, and what's the dangerous SDK alternative? *(`--append-system-prompt`; print mode (`-p`); the SDK's `customSystemPrompt`, which overwrites the default.)*

---

## Idea 11 — Technique #11: Primary Multi-Agent Delegation

**Hook.** Sub-agents report back to you. What if you fire off a *fully independent* agent that just… goes and does the job while you keep working?

**Picture.** Frame t3195 (53:15): a background Claude Code kicked off — `REPORT_FILE: ./agents/background/background-report-Sat_13_02_53.md`, "Running in the background", "When it completes it will rename the file to ...complete.md on success or ...failed.md if it fails", "1 background task" — beside the run's context bundle.

**Worked example.** Primary agents are independent Claude Code instances (own context/model/settings/keys). The lightweight version is `/background`, which builds `claude --model <m> --output-format text --dangerously-skip-permissions --append-system-prompt "<report structure + rename logic>" --print "<prompt>"` and runs it detached, writing a live report file. `scripts/bg_claude_code_test.sh` is the raw shell version. Compute orchestrating compute — out of loop, no babysitting.

**Dan's term.** *"Compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents... Better agents, and then more agents."*

**Failure mode.** Conflating background/primary delegation with sub-agents. Primary delegation gives full control (and runs on your API keys) — more power, more responsibility.

**Retrieval Q.** How is primary delegation different from sub-agents? *(Primary agents are fully independent instances with their own context/model/settings/keys and report via files; sub-agents are partially forked windows that report back to the primary agent.)*

---

## Idea 12 — Technique #12: Agent Experts

**Hook.** Encode the one engineer who knows that gnarly subsystem better than anyone — then let it maintain itself.

**Picture.** Frame t3485 (58:05): `experts/cc_hook_expert/` expanded to its three files — `cc_hook_expert_build.md`, `cc_hook_expert_improve.md`, `cc_hook_expert_plan.md` — the plan/build/improve triad that *is* the technique.

**Worked example.** A three-step expert: **plan** (writes a spec to `specs/experts/cc_hook_expert/`), **build** (implements from the spec — the demo builds `universal_hook_logger.py`), **improve** (reads the `git diff`/`git log` and updates *only* the dedicated `## Expertise` sections of the plan and build experts, never the Workflow). Evidence it works: the plan expert already carries a "Discovered Patterns from Universal Logger Implementation" block — the improve step has run. Wrap plan→build→improve→commit and you have an ADW.

**Dan's term.** *"You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge."* And the craft note: *"We're not conflating our headers"* — Expertise is its own section, distinct from Purpose/Instructions/Workflow.

**Failure mode.** Building an "expert" as a static mega-prompt and skipping the improve step, so it never self-updates and rots like any other memory file.

**Retrieval Q.** What are the three steps of an agent expert, and what makes it self-improving? *(Plan → Build → Improve; the improve step reads the git diff and updates only the dedicated `## Expertise` sections.)*

---

## Idea 13 — The future you can bet on  *(render as diagram)*

**Hook.** The reason context engineering is a *safe* bet: the models fight you as the window grows, and that won't change soon.

**Picture.** No slide — narrated over B-roll; render as a **five-card future diagram**.

**Worked example / Dan's term.** Five trends: (1) **larger** context windows (get around `/compact`); (2) **better/effective** context windows (attention-mechanism problem — capability drops as length grows); (3) **hot-swapped** context (tools/context/system-prompt, like output styles already do); (4) **multi-agent architectures** for delegation; (5) **specialized agents everywhere** (plug into the Claude Code SDK and specialize context/model/prompt/tools). Closer: *"It's not about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly"* — one-shot out-loop streaks so you can drop your presence. And don't forget prompt engineering (see the Agentic Prompt Engineering and Claude Code SDK Mastery extended lessons).

**Failure mode.** Assuming bigger future windows make this obsolete. Bigger helps; *effective* is the frontier — context engineering keeps paying off.

**Retrieval Q.** Name two future trends and the reason context engineering stays a safe bet. *(Any two of: larger / better-effective / hot-swapped context, multi-agent architectures, specialized agents; models lose capability as context grows.)*

---

## Timeline map (VTT-verified)

## Terminology glossary (Dan-isms, canonical spellings)

- **A focused agent is a performant agent** — the lesson's central law (paired with "a focused engineer is a performant engineer")
- **Context sweet spot** — the range of context where an agent performs at maximum capability
- **Core four bullseye** — right model + prompt + tools aligned with the right *range* of context
- **Search and destroy** — find context agentically, then remove/delegate it to prevent rot/bloat
- **Context rot / context bloat** — stale/contradictory context (rot) and irrelevant filler (bloat) degrading the agent
- **Context priming** — a reusable slash command that sets a task-scoped initial window (vs an always-on CLAUDE.md)

- **Agent expert** — a plan/build/improve triad that owns a codebase area and self-updates its ## Expertise

- **In-loop / out-of-loop / ZTE** — you present / agents run without you / zero-touch engineering
