# AH-1 · Elite Context Engineering — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 73:20 · Lesson #9 · Intermediate · Framework: **R&D — Reduce & Delegate**
> Lesson artifact: a 301-line README that enumerates 12 techniques across 4 levels, plus a full `.claude/` agentic layer (commands, sub-agents, hooks, output styles, an expert triad) and a two-app `apps/` playground. The whole codebase is a context-engineering exhibit.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** A focused agent is a performant agent, and there are only two ways to keep an agent focused — **Reduce** context out of your primary agent and **Delegate** context onto other agents — so master the 12 R&D techniques and you can measure, own, and scale your agents' most precious resource: the context window.

**The chapter must land the framework + 12 techniques + the future.** The framework and each technique below follow: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q. Techniques are grouped by their four levels. Two beats (Technique 9 and the future recap) are rendered as diagrams, not frames.

---

## Idea 0 — The frame: a focused agent is a performant agent (R&D)

**Hook.** You've been told models are getting smarter. True — and irrelevant if you keep drowning them. The bottleneck on a modern agent isn't intelligence; it's the state you cram into its context window. "How good are your context engineering skills? Do you have a skill issue? Let's find out and fix it."

**Picture.** Frame t0176 (2:56): the full-screen **REDUCE AND DELEGATE** title card. Frame t0266 (4:26) is the counter-image: a `/context` readout already at 63k/200k (31%) on boot, with MCP at 24.1k and a bloated memory file at 23.7k — the mess R&D exists to clean up.

**Worked example.** The entire `elite-context-engineering` repo is the framework in miniature: the README lists all 12 techniques tagged by Level (Beginner→Agentic) and Framework (Reduce/Delegate/R&D); the `.claude/` tree is the machinery (priming commands, sub-agents, hooks, output styles, an expert triad). Nothing here is application code for its own sake — it's context-engineering apparatus.

**Dan's term.** *The R&D framework — Reduce and Delegate.* Also: *a focused agent is a performant agent*, *context sweet spot*, *search and destroy*, *core four bullseye*, *context rot / context bloat*.

**Failure mode.** Hearing "context engineering" as "write a good prompt and dump in some files." The weak student never measures, never adopts the agent's perspective, and treats the window as free background plumbing — then blames the model when a bloated window underperforms.

**Retrieval Q.** What are the only two ways to manage a context window, and what's the one-line law behind them? *(Reduce and Delegate; a focused agent is a performant agent.)*

---

# LEVEL 1 — BEGINNER

## Idea 1 — Technique #1: Measure to Manage

**Hook.** You cannot manage what you cannot see. Boot a fresh Claude Code and you might already be a third full — and you'd never know it.

**Picture.** Frame t0266 (4:26): `/context` shows `claude-opus-4-1-20250805 · 63k/200k tokens (31%)`, broken down (System prompt 3.1k, System tools 11.7k, MCP tools 24.1k, Custom agents 122, Memory files 23.7k, Free 137.3k), with the IDE token counter reading `Tokens: 2650` for the README.

**Worked example.** Run `claude`, then `/context`. Install a tokenizer in your IDE so the README's ~2,650 tokens are visible *before* an agent reads it (the README is a high-touch file). Every later technique depends on this one number: how full is the window, and with what?

**Dan's term.** *"What gets measured gets managed. So measure your context window."* Tools: `/context` (what's in the window) and a token counter (what you're about to add).

**Failure mode.** Never running `/context` — "vibe coding," in Dan's words. You optimize a prompt while sitting in a 31%-full, MCP-and-memory-bloated window and can't understand why results wander.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the two measurement tools and what each tells you. *(/context = exact breakdown already in the window; a token counter = a file's cost before it enters context.)*

---

## Idea 2 — Technique #2: Avoid MCP Servers (when you don't need them)

**Hook.** The most expensive thing in your window might be tools you never call.

**Picture.** In t0266, MCP tools = 24.1k (12.1%). Frame t0505 (8:25) is the fix: after `--mcp-config` with firecrawl only, MCP drops to 6.5k (3.2%); the file tree shows the `.mcp.json.*` options.

**Worked example.** Delete the default project `.mcp.json`; avoid global (user/local) servers. Start with none, then load exactly what you need: `claude --mcp-config .mcp.json.firecrawl_7k.sample` (add `--strict-mcp-config` to override globals for that one instance). The repo ships pre-scoped configs and self-fixes the token cost in the filename so you know it up front.

**Dan's term.** *"Do not load MCP servers unless you need them."* The math: ~24k wasted per agent × five agents/hour ≈ 25% of a whole window gone.

**Failure mode.** Keeping a default `.mcp.json` "just in case," silently paying 10–12% of every agent's window for tools you don't use this session.

**Retrieval Q.** How do you load only the MCP server you need, and what flag overrides global servers? *(`claude --mcp-config <file>`; `--strict-mcp-config`.)*

---

## Idea 3 — Technique #3: More Prime, Less CLAUDE.md

**Hook.** The convenience of an always-loaded memory file is exactly what rots your window.

**Picture.** t0266 shows the `⚠ Large CLAUDE.md will impact performance (79.7k chars > 40.0k)` warning with memory files at 23.7k (11.8%). Frame t0786 (13:06): after swapping to the 43-line concise `CLAUDE.md`, memory files fall to 358 tokens (0.2%) and free space is 92.4%.

**Worked example.** `CLAUDE.large.md` (2,978 lines; header literally reads "an example of a BLOATED CLAUDE.md file... the anti-pattern of over-contextualization") vs the 43-line `CLAUDE.md`/`CLAUDE.concise.md`. Instead of a growing memory file, **prime**: `/prime` runs `git ls-files`, reads the README, reports; `/prime_cc` stacks on top to load the `.claude/` layer. Different task → different prime, so the window is always task-scoped.

**Dan's term.** *"The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason."* And: *"Prime, don't default."*

**Failure mode.** Letting CLAUDE.md grow forever into a contradictory 3,000-line glob, and reading the performance warning as noise. Contradictory context is the worst case — it actively steers the agent wrong.

**Retrieval Q.** Why is CLAUDE.md "incredible and terrible for the same reason," and what replaces it? *(It's always loaded; great for guaranteed universals, terrible because it only grows toward irrelevance/contradiction. Replace with context priming + a tiny universals-only CLAUDE.md.)*

---

# LEVEL 2 — INTERMEDIATE

## Idea 4 — Technique #4: Control Output Tokens

**Hook.** Your most expensive tokens are the ones the agent talks back to you with — and they re-enter the window.

**Picture.** Frame t1085 (18:05): left terminal `> hi` → `● Done.`; right terminal the `/output-style` menu (Default, Explanatory, Learning, Ultra Concise, One Word Output, TTS Summary, Bullet Points, YAML Structured).

**Worked example.** Output tokens cost ~3–5× input tokens. You can't cut the tokens spent *writing files*, but you can cut the *response*. The `concise-done.md` "One Word Output" style turns a ~150-token status reply into a 2-token "Done." (~99% off). Output styles hot-swap the output-style block in Claude Code's system prompt. Exceptions: questions and errors still get concise real answers.

**Dan's term.** *"Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens... a massive 99% reduction."* Note the trend teaser: *hot-swapping the system-prompt block.*

**Failure mode.** Dismissing this as trivial at one-agent scale and missing the compounding: 150 vs 2 tokens across hundreds of prompts and agents is a large, recurring drain on your most expensive tokens.

**Retrieval Q.** Why do output styles matter and roughly what was the effect shown? *(Output tokens cost 3–5×; a one-word style cut a ~150-token reply to 2 tokens, ~99%, by hot-swapping the output-style block.)*

---

## Idea 5 — Technique #5: Use Sub-Agents — Properly

**Hook.** What if you could run a big, token-hungry job and have almost none of it touch your main agent?

**Picture.** Frame t1492 (24:52): `load_ai_docs.md` (allowed-tools `Task`, firecrawl) above a terminal reading "Found 10 files... Launching docs-scraper agents…". In `/context`, Custom agents = 122 tokens (0.1%).

**Worked example.** A sub-agent's definition is a **system** prompt, so custom agents cost ~122 tokens in your primary window even though the sub-agent burns thousands doing work. `/load_ai_docs` reads `ai_docs/README.md`, deletes stale docs, and fires `docs-scraper` sub-agents in parallel via the `Task` tool — each scrape (~3k tokens) stays *off* your primary window and returns a concise report to your *primary agent* (not to you).

**Dan's term.** *"When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window."* This is the D — delegation.

**Failure mode.** Spawning sub-agents before you can track one agent's context; losing the flow of information (who prompts whom, who reports to whom). "If you're losing track of a single agent, you probably aren't ready for sub-agents."

**Retrieval Q.** Why do custom sub-agents cost only ~122 tokens in the primary window? *(They're system prompts, not user prompts, so they aren't added to the primary window; the sub-agent burns its own window and reports back to the primary agent.)*

---

## Idea 6 — Technique #6: Architect / Editor (Planner / Builder)

**Hook.** Your best code comes from an agent that never had to *find* anything — it was handed a perfect plan.

**Picture.** Frame t1790 (29:50): split screen — LEFT the planner thinking through the 3-file wrapper spec ("1. A types file... 2. A low-level file that wraps the SDK... 3. A CLI file"), RIGHT a fresh agent at `/clear` then `/build`.

**Worked example.** `/quick-plan` (the architect; `allowed-tools` Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep; writes `specs/<name>.md`) over-gathers context — *that's its job* — then a separate `/build` agent reads only the spec and implements with a clean window. The demo builds `apps/cc_ts_wrapper` (types.ts, core.ts, cli.ts), a Claude Code TypeScript SDK wrapper, from the plan. "You go overboard planning, then delete."

**Dan's term.** *Architect and editor / planner and builder.* Shout-out to legacy AI-coding tools (Aider) that separated planning from building.

**Failure mode.** Prompt-chaining inside one chat window instead of splitting responsibilities, causing context rot with every non-focused prompt and denying the builder a clean window for surgical edits.

**Retrieval Q.** In the architect/editor split, whose job is it to "waste" tokens, and why? *(The planner's — it over-gathers to write a complete spec; you then delete the irrelevant parts so the builder gets a focused window.)*

---

# LEVEL 3 — ADVANCED

## Idea 7 — Technique #7: Avoid /compact — Reset and Prime

**Hook.** After `/compact`, quick — what's in your window right now? You don't know. Neither does Dan.

**Picture.** Frame t2050 (34:10): the builder's finished `cc_ts_wrapper` report (types.ts/core.ts/cli.ts + "Git diff stats: 1 file changed") followed by `> /compact` → "Compacting conversation…".

**Worked example.** `/compact` is a bandaid: it summarizes and leaves an *unknown* state you must Ctrl-R to reread. Instead, `/clear` (blow the window away completely) then `/prime` (reload exactly what you want). You trade a little work for certainty — and it prepares you for out-loop coding, where no single agent should overflow 200k and trigger a compaction you can't predict. If it would, chop up the task.

**Dan's term.** *"When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing... I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime."* And: *"You don't want to delegate the control of your context window."*

**Failure mode.** Reaching for `/compact` reflexively and never knowing the exact window — fine in-loop, fatal the moment you try to scale out-of-loop where predictability is everything.

**Retrieval Q.** Why does Dan avoid `/compact`, and what does he do instead? *(You don't know exactly what's retained; `/clear` then `/prime` so you own and know your exact state.)*

---

## Idea 8 — Technique #8: Use Context Bundles

**Hook.** When an agent's window finally explodes, you don't have to start from zero — you can hand its replacement the story so far.

**Picture.** Frame t2345 (39:05): the `agents/context_bundles/` directory full of `SAT_<hour>_<session>.jsonl` files; one open shows `{"operation":"prompt","prompt":"/prime_cc"}`, `{"operation":"read","file_path":".claude/settings.json"}`, ...; the terminal replays deduped reads.

**Worked example.** A `PostToolUse` hook (`context_bundle_builder.py`) writes an append-only JSONL log of prompts/reads (with limit/offset)/writes to `agents/context_bundles/<DAY_HOUR>_<session_id>.jsonl`. A fresh agent runs `/load_bundle <path>`, which dedups reads (full file if any entry lacks a limit) and replays ~60–70% of the prior agent's state and story — without every detail. Use it selectively.

**Dan's term.** *Context bundle* — *"a simple append-only log of the work that our Claude Code instances are doing... this gets us 70% of where the previous agent was."*

**Failure mode.** Logging every operation and reloading the whole thing — which just overflows the next agent. The trimmed, deduped replay is the point.

**Retrieval Q.** What produces a context bundle and what reloads it? *(A Claude Code hook, `context_bundle_builder.py`, writes per-session JSONL; `/load_bundle` dedups and replays it.)*

---

## Idea 9 — Technique #9: Use One Agent for One Purpose  *(render as diagram)*

**Hook.** The simplest, most powerful rule, and the one that turns techniques into a system: ship one thing at a time.

**Picture.** No unique UI — render as a designed **agent-pipeline (ADW) diagram**: a high-level prompt fanning into single-purpose agents (plan → build → improve → commit).

**Worked example.** It summarizes everything before it. Two-step problem solving: (1) plan the work with *no regard for technology* (users/customers first), then (2) plan how to delegate it across single-purpose agents — an agentic pipeline / AI Developer Workflow (the highest leverage in agentic coding, and the key idea of TAC Lesson 6).

**Dan's term.** *"Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused."* The pipeline is the *ADW*.

**Failure mode.** Making one capable agent own a whole feature; its window rots and you can't tell which part failed. Single-purpose agents localize both focus and debugging.

**Retrieval Q.** What two planning steps does "one agent, one purpose" force? *(Plan the work without regard for technology; then plan the agent pipeline / ADW to deliver it.)*

---

# LEVEL 4 — AGENTIC (the hidden level)

> "Many engineers will not get to this level. Many engineers don't need this level." Here your patterns scale into your ADWs — powerful and dangerous.

## Idea 10 — Technique #10: Modify the System Prompt

**Hook.** Beneath output styles is the real control surface: the system prompt itself.

**Picture.** Frame t2705 (45:05): one command line — `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model sonnet --append-system-prompt "IMPORTANT: When using the Read tool, ALWAYS read in increments of 100 lines... prefix your last message with ✅ or ❌..." -p "what is CLAUDE.large.md for?"`.

**Worked example.** Two knobs: `--append-system-prompt` (adds to Claude Code's crafted default) and the SDK's `customSystemPrompt` (a full *overwrite* — dangerous). Appending must run in **print mode** (`-p`, out-loop). The demo forces the read tool into 100-line increments and a ✅/❌ final-message prefix; the run's context bundle proves obedience — `Read(100)`, `Read(100)` — reducing lines read (and tokens). Points to the Claude Code SDK Mastery extended lesson.

**Dan's term.** *"When you control the behavior, you control the context window."* And the warning: *"Do not use [customSystemPrompt] unless you know what you're doing."*

**Failure mode.** Grabbing `customSystemPrompt` and blowing away the carefully crafted default system prompt. Use `--append-system-prompt` unless you truly need a replacement.

**Retrieval Q.** Which flag appends to the system prompt, what mode is required, and what's the dangerous SDK alternative? *(`--append-system-prompt`; print mode (`-p`); the SDK's `customSystemPrompt`, which overwrites the default.)*

---

## Idea 11 — Technique #11: Primary Multi-Agent Delegation

**Hook.** Sub-agents report back to you. What if you fire off a *fully independent* agent that just… goes and does the job while you keep working?

**Picture.** Frame t3195 (53:15): a background Claude Code kicked off — `REPORT_FILE: ./agents/background/background-report-Sat_13_02_53.md`, "Running in the background", "When it completes it will rename the file to ...complete.md on success or ...failed.md if it fails", "1 background task" — beside the run's context bundle.

**Worked example.** Primary agents are independent Claude Code instances (own context/model/settings/keys). The lightweight version is `/background`, which builds `claude --model <m> --output-format text --dangerously-skip-permissions --append-system-prompt "<report structure + rename logic>" --print "<prompt>"` and runs it detached, writing a live report file. `scripts/bg_claude_code_test.sh` is the raw shell version. Compute orchestrating compute — out of loop, no babysitting.

**Dan's term.** *"Compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents... Better agents, and then more agents."*

**Failure mode.** Conflating background/primary delegation with sub-agents. Primary delegation gives full control (and runs on your API keys) — more power, more responsibility.

**Retrieval Q.** How is primary delegation different from sub-agents? *(Primary agents are fully independent instances with their own context/model/settings/keys and report via files; sub-agents are partially forked windows that report back to the primary agent.)*

---

## Idea 12 — Technique #12: Agent Experts

**Hook.** Encode the one engineer who knows that gnarly subsystem better than anyone — then let it maintain itself.

**Picture.** Frame t3485 (58:05): `experts/cc_hook_expert/` expanded to its three files — `cc_hook_expert_build.md`, `cc_hook_expert_improve.md`, `cc_hook_expert_plan.md` — the plan/build/improve triad that *is* the technique.

**Worked example.** A three-step expert: **plan** (writes a spec to `specs/experts/cc_hook_expert/`), **build** (implements from the spec — the demo builds `universal_hook_logger.py`), **improve** (reads the `git diff`/`git log` and updates *only* the dedicated `## Expertise` sections of the plan and build experts, never the Workflow). Evidence it works: the plan expert already carries a "Discovered Patterns from Universal Logger Implementation" block — the improve step has run. Wrap plan→build→improve→commit and you have an ADW.

**Dan's term.** *"You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge."* And the craft note: *"We're not conflating our headers"* — Expertise is its own section, distinct from Purpose/Instructions/Workflow.

**Failure mode.** Building an "expert" as a static mega-prompt and skipping the improve step, so it never self-updates and rots like any other memory file.

**Retrieval Q.** What are the three steps of an agent expert, and what makes it self-improving? *(Plan → Build → Improve; the improve step reads the git diff and updates only the dedicated `## Expertise` sections.)*

---

## Idea 13 — The future you can bet on  *(render as diagram)*

**Hook.** The reason context engineering is a *safe* bet: the models fight you as the window grows, and that won't change soon.

**Picture.** No slide — narrated over B-roll; render as a **five-card future diagram**.

**Worked example / Dan's term.** Five trends: (1) **larger** context windows (get around `/compact`); (2) **better/effective** context windows (attention-mechanism problem — capability drops as length grows); (3) **hot-swapped** context (tools/context/system-prompt, like output styles already do); (4) **multi-agent architectures** for delegation; (5) **specialized agents everywhere** (plug into the Claude Code SDK and specialize context/model/prompt/tools). Closer: *"It's not about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly"* — one-shot out-loop streaks so you can drop your presence. And don't forget prompt engineering (see the Agentic Prompt Engineering and Claude Code SDK Mastery extended lessons).

**Failure mode.** Assuming bigger future windows make this obsolete. Bigger helps; *effective* is the frontier — context engineering keeps paying off.

**Retrieval Q.** Name two future trends and the reason context engineering stays a safe bet. *(Any two of: larger / better-effective / hot-swapped context, multi-agent architectures, specialized agents; models lose capability as context grows.)*

# AH-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of your agentic-coding practice breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is the framework you cannot skip; Tier 2 is the working machinery (the 12 techniques, distilled); Tier 3 is framing that keeps you honest and moving. The loot box ships 18 notes — these fold them in and rank them.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. A focused agent is a performant agent.**
Focus isn't tidiness — it's the *mechanism* of performance. A clean, task-scoped window makes better, more surgical decisions and one-shots more often than a bloated one. Everything else is in service of this.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds like a slogan. It's a testable claim — measure the window, then judge the output against it.

**2. There are only two moves: Reduce and Delegate (R&D).**
**Reduce** = strip context out of your *primary* agent. **Delegate** = push context onto *other* agents. Every one of the 12 techniques is one or both. If you can sort a technique into R or D, you understand it.
*Say it Dan's way:* "When you boil it down, there are only two ways to manage your context window, R and D. Reduce and delegate."

**3. Measure before you manage: `/context` + a token counter.**
`/context` shows what's already in the window (system prompt, tools, MCP, agents, memory, messages, free). A tokenizer shows a file's cost *before* it enters. On camera a fresh boot was already 31% full. If you never run `/context`, you're vibe coding.

**4. Own your context window — never hand its control away.**
Not to a bloated CLAUDE.md, not to `/compact`, not to any tool. You own your prompt and your model; own your context the same way. This single principle generates half the techniques (prime not default; clear-and-prime not compact; append-system-prompt to steer the read tool).

---

## Tier 2 — The 12 techniques, distilled (the working machinery)

**5. (T2) Delete the default `.mcp.json`.**
Preloaded MCP servers cost 10–12% of your window on every agent you boot (24.1k tokens on camera). Load only what you need: `claude --mcp-config <file>` (+ `--strict-mcp-config` to beat globals). Five agents/hour × 24k ≈ a quarter of a window wasted.

**6. (T3) Prime, don't default.**
CLAUDE.md is incredible AND terrible for the same reason — it's *always loaded*. Shrink it to true universals (43 lines / 0.2%); use `/prime`, `/prime_cc`, `/prime_bug`… to load task-scoped context on demand. The bloated `CLAUDE.large.md` (2,978 lines) trips Claude Code's own "will impact performance" warning.

**7. (T4) Cap output tokens with output styles.**
Output tokens cost 3–5× input and re-enter the window. A one-word "Done." style cut a ~150-token reply to 2 tokens (~99%). Output styles hot-swap the output-style block in the system prompt. Small per call; huge across hundreds of agents.

**8. (T5) Sub-agents are partially forked windows.**
A sub-agent is a *system* prompt, so custom agents cost ~122 tokens in your primary window while the sub-agent burns its own thousands. `/load_ai_docs` fans out `docs-scraper` sub-agents in parallel and keeps the scrape *off* your primary agent. Caveat: you now track every agent's core four.

**9. (T6) Split the architect from the editor.**
One agent plans (`/quick-plan` → a spec), a *fresh* agent builds (`/build` the spec). The planner is *supposed* to over-gather — "go overboard, then delete" — so the builder gets a clean window for surgical, error-free edits. Don't prompt-chain in one chat window; that's how rot creeps in.

**10. (T7) Reset and prime — don't `/compact`.**
After `/compact` you don't know what's in your window (Ctrl-R to find out). `/clear` then `/prime` leaves a *known* state you own. Out-loop, no single agent should overflow 200k and trigger a compaction you can't predict — if it would, chop up the task.

**11. (T8) Context bundles remount an exploded agent.**
A hook writes an append-only JSONL trail of prompts/reads/writes to `agents/context_bundles/<DAY_HOUR>_<session>.jsonl`. A fresh agent runs `/load_bundle` to dedup and replay ~70% of the prior agent's state. Don't log everything — the trimmed replay is the point.

**12. (T9) One agent, one purpose.**
The summary technique. Plan the work with *no regard for technology*, then plan the *pipeline* of single-purpose agents (an ADW). A focused agent is a performant agent — so give each one exactly one job, and debugging localizes to one piece.

**13. (T10) `--append-system-prompt` steers behavior (print mode only).**
Append to the crafted default (don't overwrite it with the SDK's `customSystemPrompt`). The demo forced "read in 100-line increments" + a ✅/❌ final prefix; the context bundle proved it — `Read(100), Read(100)`. Control behavior → control the window.

**14. (T11) Fire independent primary agents (e.g. `/background`).**
Unlike sub-agents, a background agent is a *full* Claude Code instance (own context/model/settings/keys) that writes a report file and renames it `.complete.md`/`.failed.md`. Compute orchestrating compute — out of loop, no babysitting.

**15. (T12) Agent experts: plan → build → improve, self-updating.**
Specialized agents that own a codebase area *and* auto-update their own knowledge: the **improve** step reads the `git diff` and edits *only* the dedicated `## Expertise` sections (never the Workflow). Encode the engineer who knows that subsystem — and let it maintain itself. Wrap it into an ADW.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**16. Adopt your agent's perspective.**
Stop reasoning from your convenience; reason about *this agent's* window right now. Awareness of each agent's state inside your pipelines is what separates context engineering from vibe coding.

**17. It's not about saving tokens — it's about spending them properly.**
The goal isn't a low bill; it's not wasting time and tokens *correcting* the agent. Aim for one-shot out-loop streaks with the fewest attempts, so you can drop your presence.

**18. Context engineering is a safe bet.**
Models lose capability as the window grows (an attention problem). That won't change soon, so investing your time in context management pays off regardless of model or window size. Bet on it — and don't forget prompt engineering; bad prompts waste a perfect context.

**19. This is not vibe coding — you have to invest.**
"If it's easy, a vibe coder is probably doing it, and that isn't irreplaceable." Even one technique saves real time; you have twelve. Pick a couple, deploy them, measure the difference.

**20. Better agents, then more agents.**
Make one agent better = master its window (Reduce). Add more agents = delegation to the max, one purpose each (Delegate). The endgame is in-loop → out-of-loop → ZTE.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. R&D — what do the letters stand for, and sort five techniques into the two buckets.
2. Two tools to measure context, and what a fresh `/context` boot showed on camera.
3. Why is CLAUDE.md "incredible and terrible for the same reason"? What replaces it?
4. Why do sub-agents cost only ~122 tokens in your primary window?
5. Why avoid `/compact`, and what's the two-command alternative?
6. What produces a context bundle, and what reloads it?
7. Which flag appends to the system prompt, what mode is required, and what's the dangerous SDK alternative?
8. Name the three steps of an agent expert and what makes it self-improving.

*(Answers: nuggets/extract Idea 0, 3/T1, T3, T5, T7, T8, T10, T12.)*

# AH-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

AH-1 ages well because it teaches *principles of context* (measure, reduce, delegate, own your window) on top of tool features that keep evolving. Dan future-proofs on camera repeatedly: *"You might have a model in the future... context management is still critically important"* and *"these techniques are all the same across models. Don't get stuck up on any one individual model."* Six things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.

---

## 1. Reusable expertise: hand-rolled Agent Experts → first-class Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap

**Course era:** Technique #12 encodes reusable expertise as a plan/build/improve slash-command triad with a hand-maintained `## Expertise` section, self-updated by an `improve` meta-command reading the `git diff`. Brilliant, but discovery, loading, and sharing are all hand-rolled.
**Current:** Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` with frontmatter — name, description, trigger guidance) are the first-class encoding: discovered and loaded on demand, shareable across projects/teams, composable. They're the modern answer to "how do I package what my agent knows about this subsystem?" — exactly what the expert triad answers primitively.
**Book treatment:** overlay + sidebar. Teach the codebase's plan/build/improve triad first (no magic, and the self-updating loop is genuinely additive), then show the same idea as a Skill.
**Overlay:** an IndyDevDan Skills/hooks video (`corrects outdated`; include_in_phase1: **yes**) — ID needs sourcing (see note).

## 2. Embedding: bare `--append-system-prompt`/`--print` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK

**Course era:** Techniques #10–11 use CLI flags — `--append-system-prompt`, `--print`, `--output-format text`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `run_in_background=true` — and `scripts/bg_claude_code_test.sh` as the raw shell form.
**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the clearest teaching form), but production embedding adds richer headless flags (`--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume) and the **Claude Agent SDK** (Python/TS): structured output, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. The lesson itself points you to the "Claude Code SDK Mastery" extended lesson for this.
**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the flag you just used has a grown-up SDK form"), not a rewrite — the concept (agent as callable, steerable component) is unchanged.
**Overlay:** a Claude Code / Agent SDK video (`named hole`; include_in_phase1: **yes**) — ID needs sourcing.

## 3. Output styles → a broader customization surface

**Course era:** Technique #4 teaches output styles that "hot-swap the output-style block in the system prompt" (One Word Output, Ultra Concise, TTS, Bullet Points, YAML Structured), selected via `/output-style` or `settings.local.*.json`.
**Current:** output styles still exist, but Claude Code's customization surface has broadened (plugins, settings layering, and Skills sit alongside output styles). Dan explicitly names *hot-swapping the system-prompt block* as a trend to watch — and it broadly played out.
**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout; the durable point is "control the response layer to cap your most expensive (output) tokens."
**Overlay:** none required.

## 4. Models & the on-screen numbers: period detail, pre-handled by Dan

**Course era:** `/context` shows `claude-opus-4-1-20250805` and `claude-sonnet-4-20250514`; `quick-plan.md` pins `model: claude-opus-4-1-20250805`; token breakdowns (63k boot, 24.1k MCP, 23.7k memory, 6.5k firecrawl, 2,650 README) are record-time exact.
**Current:** newer model families (Claude 5 / Opus 4.x era); token accounting shifts with model and tool changes. None of it invalidates a technique — the demo is about *proportions and habits*, not specific counts.
**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected frames ("model ids and counts are period detail; the technique is identical today"). Update the pinned model id when adapting the codebase. No overlay.

## 5. Repo state on camera ≠ shipped repo (MCP sample filenames)

**Course era:** the on-screen file tree shows `.mcp.json.all_22k`, `.mcp.json.firecrawl_4k`, and `.mcp.json.empty`.
**Current/shipped:** the repo ships `.mcp.json.all_16k.sample`, `.mcp.json.firecrawl_7k.sample`, and `.mcp.json.sample` (no `.empty`). The self-fixed token counts baked into filenames (4k/7k/16k/22k) reflect the MCP surface at record time vs ship time.
**Book treatment:** teach from the *shipped* filenames; footnote the on-screen names/numbers as record-time detail. Not a defect — a snapshot difference.
**Overlay:** none.

## 6. `/compact` vs reset-and-prime: a stance, and compaction keeps improving

**Course era:** Technique #7 is deliberately opinionated — avoid `/compact`, `/clear` + `/prime` instead, because after compaction you don't know your exact state.
**Current:** `/compact` remains a legitimate built-in and has grown (custom summarization instructions, auto-compact). The *durable* lesson is "know and own your exact window state, especially out-loop"; the specific avoidance is a tunable practice as compaction gets more controllable.
**Book treatment:** present as Dan's reasoned stance with the "own your window" principle foregrounded; note that compaction tooling has improved. No overlay.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)

- **The R&D framework.** Reduce and Delegate is a complete, model-agnostic taxonomy for context management.
- **A focused agent is a performant agent.** More true as fleets scale, not less.
- **Measure to manage.** `/context` + a tokenizer remain the two right instruments; the "you can't manage what you don't measure" logic is timeless.
- **The context sweet spot / attention-vs-length problem.** Models still lose capability as windows grow — the reason context engineering is "a safe bet."
- **Own your context window.** Don't delegate its control to a memory file or a compactor. Unchanged.
- **Sub-agents as partially forked (system-prompt-isolated) windows; primary delegation as independent instances.** The distinction and its token economics hold.
- **Architect/editor split; one agent, one purpose; compose into ADWs.** The pipeline logic is the backbone of current multi-agent practice.
- **Self-improving experts (plan/build/improve, update only the Expertise section).** The *loop* is current even as Skills become the packaging.
- **Spend tokens properly, not minimally.** The reliability framing (avoid re-work, one-shot out-loop) is exactly today's cost logic.

## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3 include_in_phase1)

| # | Candidate (topic) | Maps to | Include | ID status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | IndyDevDan — context engineering / context-window management | operationalizes tactic (whole thesis) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 2 | IndyDevDan — Claude Code sub-agents / delegation | named hole (T5/T11 current practice) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 3 | IndyDevDan — hooks / Agent Skills / Agent SDK | corrects outdated (T8/T10/T12 → Skills+SDK) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 4 | IndyDevDan — AI Developer Workflows / multi-agent orchestration | named hole (T9 → ADW at scale) | ❌ defer | needs sourcing |

**Critical caveat (per brief + no-fabrication rule):** AH-1 had **no seeded overlay list** in `data/curriculum.json` (`overlays: []`) and the chapter brief provided none. I have **not invented YouTube IDs**. Each phase-1 candidate is a *topic to source*: the chapter build/review stage must find the real IndyDevDan video, confirm the ID resolves via oembed, and verify the content matches the mapped role before publishing the overlay link (exactly as TAC-1's cross-review did for its seeded IDs). Keep `include_in_phase1` to at most 3.

- **The R&D framework.** Reduce and Delegate is a complete, model-agnostic taxonomy for context management.
- **A focused agent is a performant agent.** More true as fleets scale, not less.
- **Measure to manage.** `/context` + a tokenizer remain the two right instruments; the "you can't manage what you don't measure" logic is timeless.
- **The context sweet spot / attention-vs-length problem.** Models still lose capability as windows grow — the reason context engineering is "a safe bet."
- **Own your context window.** Don't delegate its control to a memory file or a compactor. Unchanged.
- **Sub-agents as partially forked (system-prompt-isolated) windows; primary delegation as independent instances.** The distinction and its token economics hold.
- **Architect/editor split; one agent, one purpose; compose into ADWs.** The pipeline logic is the backbone of current multi-agent practice.
- **Self-improving experts (plan/build/improve, update only the Expertise section).** The *loop* is current even as Skills become the packaging.
- **Spend tokens properly, not minimally.** The reliability framing (avoid re-work, one-shot out-loop) is exactly today's cost logic.

| # | Candidate (topic) | Maps to | Include | ID status |

| 1 | IndyDevDan — context engineering / context-window management | operationalizes tactic (whole thesis) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 2 | IndyDevDan — Claude Code sub-agents / delegation | named hole (T5/T11 current practice) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 3 | IndyDevDan — hooks / Agent Skills / Agent SDK | corrects outdated (T8/T10/T12 → Skills+SDK) | ✅ | needs sourcing + oembed-verify |
| 4 | IndyDevDan — AI Developer Workflows / multi-agent orchestration | named hole (T9 → ADW at scale) | ❌ defer | needs sourcing |

**Critical caveat (per brief + no-fabrication rule):** AH-1 had **no seeded overlay list** in `data/curriculum.json` (`overlays: []`) and the chapter brief provided none. I have **not invented YouTube IDs**. Each phase-1 candidate is a *topic to source*: the chapter build/review stage must find the real IndyDevDan video, confirm the ID resolves via oembed, and verify the content matches the mapped role before publishing the overlay link (exactly as TAC-1's cross-review did for its seeded IDs). Keep `include_in_phase1` to at most 3.

# AH-1 Lab Spec — Elite Context Engineering (the R&D Framework)

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `agentic-horizon/elite-context-engineering`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/elite-context-engineering.git`). No external repos.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you MEASURE with `/context` before and after every reduce/delegate move, and you can cite the numbers. The graded outcome is that you can *see, own, and move* your window — not just run commands. Corollary: zero application code typed by hand (the wrapper and the hook come from planner/builder/expert agents).
**Time box:** 75–120 minutes (12 techniques). Token cost: real but modest at beginner/intermediate; the agentic-level drills (10–12) bill directly on your API key — budget for it.

---

## 0 · Setup + baseline measurement (10 min)

1. `git clone https://github.com/disler/elite-context-engineering.git && cd elite-context-engineering`
2. Open in an IDE with a **token-counter extension** in the status bar (Dan uses VS Code). Copy `.env.sample` → `.env` and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (ELEVENLABS/OPENAI optional, only for the TTS/util demos).
3. Read `README.md`: note all 12 techniques with their **Level** (Beginner→Agentic) and **Framework** (Reduce/Delegate/R&D) tags, and the bash aliases at the bottom (`cld`, `cldys`, `cldyo`, `lfg`, …).
4. Boot `claude`, run `/context`, and **write down the boot state**: total %, System tools, MCP tools, Custom agents, Memory files, Free space.

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state your boot-state numbers and what each `/context` line means. If you can't read the window, you can't manage it.

## 1 · REDUCE — beginner level (Techniques 1–3, 20 min)

**T1 Measure.** With the README open, watch the IDE token counter (~2,650 tokens). Re-run `/context`; identify the two biggest consumers (on Dan's machine: MCP tools 24.1k and Memory files 23.7k).

**T2 Avoid MCP.** Confirm the default MCP cost. Then relaunch loading only what you need:
`claude --mcp-config .mcp.json.firecrawl_7k.sample --strict-mcp-config`
Re-run `/context`; verify MCP tokens dropped (Dan's went 24.1k → 6.5k). Say out loud why `--strict-mcp-config` matters (it overrides global user/local servers).

**T3 Prime > CLAUDE.md.** Point the project at the bloated memory file (`CLAUDE.large.md`, 2,978 lines) and observe the `⚠ Large CLAUDE.md will impact performance` warning + Memory-files %. Restore the 43-line `CLAUDE.md`/`CLAUDE.concise.md`; confirm Memory files fall to ~0.2% and Free space ~90%+. Then `/prime` (git ls-files → read README → report) and inspect `/prime_cc`.

**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** MCP tokens AND memory-file tokens both measurably dropped, verified in `/context`. State which lever (delete/scope MCP; shrink+prime) reduced each, and which R it is (all Reduce).

## 2 · REDUCE + DELEGATE — intermediate level (Techniques 4–6, 20 min)

**T4 Output tokens.** Open two terminals. Set one to the **One Word Output** style (via `settings.local.concise.json` or `/output-style` → "One Word Output"); leave the other default. Send the same prompt to both (start with `hi`, then "What does this codebase do?"). Compare the response token counts — the concise one should say roughly "Done." (a few tokens) vs a full paragraph.

**T5 Sub-agents.** In `/context`, note **Custom agents ≈ 122 tokens** (they're system prompts). Run `/load_ai_docs`; watch it read `ai_docs/README.md`, delete docs >24h old, and fire `docs-scraper` sub-agents in parallel. Confirm the scrape tokens did **not** land on your primary window (`/context` afterward).

**T6 Architect/Editor.** `/quick-plan "add a tiny helper to apps/cc_ts_wrapper"` (writes `specs/<name>.md`). Open a **fresh** agent and `/build <path-to-spec>`. Confirm the builder needed no priming — everything was in the plan.

**Checkpoint 2:** (a) the concise style produced a measurably smaller response than default; (b) `/load_ai_docs` kept scrape work off your primary window; (c) a fresh `/build` agent implemented from the spec alone. State which technique is Reduce, which is Delegate, and which is both.

## 3 · Advanced level (Techniques 7–9, 20 min)

**T7 Avoid /compact.** After some work, run `/compact`, then `Ctrl-R` to read the summary — notice you had to *look* to know your state. Now do the alternative: `/clear` then `/prime`. Write one sentence on which leaves you *knowing* your exact window.

**T8 Context bundles.** Inspect `agents/context_bundles/<DAY_HOUR>_<session>.jsonl` (built by the `PostToolUse`/`UserPromptSubmit` hook `context_bundle_builder.py`). Re-run `/prime` and watch entries append. In a fresh agent, `/load_bundle <path>` and confirm deduped replay of the prior agent's reads.

**T9 One agent, one purpose.** On paper, take one real task and split it into a pipeline of single-purpose agents (plan → build → improve → commit). No code — just the pipeline. This is the ADW you'll automate in later lessons.

**Checkpoint 3:** you can explain why `/clear`+`/prime` leaves a known state and `/compact` doesn't, and a fresh agent successfully remounted prior state via `/load_bundle`.

## 4 · Agentic level (Techniques 10–12, 25 min — bills on your API key)

**T10 System prompt.** Run in print mode:
`claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model sonnet --append-system-prompt "ALWAYS read files in 100-line increments (offset=0 limit=100, then offset=100 limit=100); if you have enough, stop and proceed; prefix your final message with ✅ or ❌" -p "what is CLAUDE.large.md for?"`
Open the resulting context bundle and confirm `Read(..., limit:100)` operations — the append-system-prompt steered the read tool itself.

**T11 Primary delegation.** From a primary agent: `/background "/quick-plan add a second helper to the wrapper" sonnet`. Watch `agents/background/background-report-*.md` get written and renamed to `.complete.md` (or `.failed.md`). You did not sit in the loop.

**T12 Agent experts.** Run the triad on a tiny hook feature:
`/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_plan "log SessionStart events to a JSONL file"` → `/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_build <spec-path>` → `/experts:cc_hook_expert:cc_hook_expert_improve`.
Confirm via `git diff` that **improve** edited **only** the `## Expertise` sections of the plan/build experts (never the Workflow).

**Checkpoint 4:** (a) the context bundle shows 100-line reads; (b) a `/background` agent wrote and renamed its report without you; (c) the improve step updated only the Expertise section (git diff proves Workflow untouched).

## Stretch drills (still zero hand-typing)

- **S1 — New prime area.** Author `/prime_bug` (or `/prime_feature`) that primes a different focus; prove via `/context` it loads a different, task-scoped window than `/prime`.
- **S2 — New self-fixed MCP config.** Add a `.mcp.json.<server>_<Nk>.sample` for a server you actually use; load it with `--strict-mcp-config` and confirm the token cost matches the filename.
- **S3 — New output style.** Create a style between "One Word Output" and default (one line + a status emoji); measure the response-token delta on a fixed prompt.
- **S4 — Second expert.** Create a new expert triad (plan/build/improve) for another codebase concern; run improve after a change and verify it updates only the Expertise section.
- **S5 — Wrap an ADW.** Chain plan → build → improve → `git commit` as a single background workflow, using a context bundle to remount if a step overflows.

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] You measured with `/context` before and after every reduce/delegate move and can cite the numbers (Checkpoints 0–4).
- [ ] MCP-tool and memory-file token usage measurably dropped (Reduce), verified in `/context`.
- [ ] You delegated at least twice — sub-agents via `/load_ai_docs` and a primary `/background` agent — keeping work off your primary window.
- [ ] You ran the architect/editor split and the agent-experts plan/build/improve loop end to end.
- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand (the wrapper and the hook came from planner/builder/expert agents).
- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: name the R&D framework; sort all 12 techniques into their Level and into Reduce vs Delegate; state the central law ("a focused agent is a performant agent"); and explain the paradox — how spending MORE effort on context (reset-and-prime, plan-then-build, maintain experts) lets you do LESS babysitting and drop your presence.

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall — not measuring.** Students run the commands but never open `/context`, so they can't see the payoff. Make every checkpoint a *number*, not a vibe.
- **Second stall — model/count drift.** The recording shows `claude-opus-4-1-20250805`, MCP `24.1k`, README `2,650`, and on-screen `.mcp.json.all_22k`/`.firecrawl_4k`. The shipped repo uses `.mcp.json.all_16k.sample`/`.firecrawl_7k.sample`, and your models/counts will differ. That's expected — grade the *direction and proportion* of the change, not exact figures.
- **Third stall — quick-plan model pin.** `quick-plan.md` pins a course-era Opus id (`claude-opus-4-1-20250805`); if that model isn't available, update the frontmatter to a current model before running T6/T11.
- **Cost anxiety.** Beginner/intermediate drills are cheap; the agentic-level drills (10–12) and any background/expert runs bill on your API key. If a student can't run them, the pay-to-play conversation is the lesson surfacing early — do the read-only inspection of the codebase files instead.
- **Guardrails.** `--dangerously-skip-permissions` and `/background` run with reduced safety and on your keys; keep them scoped to this repo and small prompts. Do not point background/expert agents at unrelated directories.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** full ADW orchestration at scale, worktree-parallel fleets, and the Claude Agent SDK — those are later TAC/AH lessons and the Claude Code SDK Mastery extended lesson. Keep the 12 primitives crisp; deflect scope creep.

    { "text": "If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding, and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "5:13" },
    { "text": "Do not load MCP servers unless you need them... it's very likely you're wasting tokens with MCP servers you're not actively using.", "approx_timestamp": "5:50" },
    { "text": "The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason.", "approx_timestamp": "13:35" },
    { "text": "So prime, don't default. Your CLAUDE.md file should be shrunk to contain only the absolute universal essentials that you're 100% sure you want loaded 100% of the time.", "approx_timestamp": "14:55" },
    { "text": "Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens.", "approx_timestamp": "16:37" },
    { "text": "When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window.", "approx_timestamp": "22:55" },
    { "text": "There's only two ways to manage your context window: reduce context entering your primary agent, and delegate context to sub-agents and to other primary agents.", "approx_timestamp": "26:20" },
    { "text": "By the end of your planning phase, you should be deleting information that isn't relevant to the work you want done. You should go overboard, then delete.", "approx_timestamp": "32:10" },
    { "text": "When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing. I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime.", "approx_timestamp": "34:14" },
    { "text": "You don't want to delegate the control of your context window. You want to own this, just like you want to control your prompt or your model.", "approx_timestamp": "36:00" },
    { "text": "Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused. A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "42:50" },
    { "text": "The system prompt really lets you start controlling how your agent behaves, and when you control the behavior, you control the context window.", "approx_timestamp": "45:40" },
    { "text": "We are kicking off a Claude Code instance from Claude Code. We have compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents. This is where everything is headed. Better agents, and then more agents.", "approx_timestamp": "52:10" },
    { "text": "You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge. This is the agent experts technique.", "approx_timestamp": "57:34" },
    { "text": "It's not necessarily about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly. We manage our context window so that we don't waste time and tokens correcting our agents' mistakes.", "approx_timestamp": "68:38" },
    { "text": "It's a safe bet to bet on context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "70:00" },
    { "text": "A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "73:08", "source": "sign-off" }

    { "q": "Name the two tools for measuring context and what each shows.", "a": "/context (exact breakdown already in the window — system prompt, tools, MCP, agents, memory, messages, free space) and an IDE token counter/tokenizer (a file's token cost BEFORE it enters context)." },
    { "q": "Roughly how much of the window did MCP tools consume in the demo, and how do you load only what you need?", "a": "~24.1k tokens (~12%). Delete the default .mcp.json and use `claude --mcp-config <file>` (add `--strict-mcp-config` to override global servers)." },
    { "q": "Why is CLAUDE.md 'incredible and terrible for the same reason'?", "a": "Because it's always loaded. Great for guaranteed universals; terrible because it only grows and eventually carries irrelevant or contradictory context. Fix: shrink it to true universals and prime dynamically." },
    { "q": "Why do output styles matter, and what's the scale of the effect shown?", "a": "Output tokens cost 3-5x input and re-enter context. A one-word 'Done.' style cut a ~150-token reply to 2 tokens (~99%) by hot-swapping the output-style block in the system prompt." },
    { "q": "Why do custom sub-agents cost only ~122 tokens in the primary window?", "a": "A sub-agent's definition is a SYSTEM prompt, not a user prompt, so it isn't added to the primary agent's context window; the sub-agent burns its OWN window doing the work and returns a concise report to the primary agent." },
    { "q": "In the architect/editor split, whose job is it to 'waste' tokens, and why?", "a": "The planner/architect's — it over-gathers context to write a complete spec, then you delete the irrelevant parts so the builder/editor gets a clean, focused window for surgical edits." },
    { "q": "Why does Dan avoid /compact, and what does he do instead?", "a": "After /compact you don't know exactly what's in your window (you must Ctrl-R and reread). Instead /clear then /prime, so you own and know your exact state — essential for out-loop scale." },

    { "q": "Which flag modifies the system prompt, what mode must it run in, and what SDK variable is the dangerous alternative?", "a": "--append-system-prompt, run in print mode (-p / out-loop); the SDK's customSystemPrompt fully OVERWRITES the default system prompt (use with caution)." },
    { "q": "How is primary multi-agent delegation different from sub-agents?", "a": "Primary agents are fully independent Claude Code instances with their own context, model, settings, and keys (e.g. /background writing a report file); sub-agents are partially forked context windows that report back to the primary agent." },
    { "q": "What are the three steps of an agent expert, and what makes it self-improving?", "a": "Plan → Build → Improve. Improve reads the git diff/status and updates ONLY the dedicated ## Expertise sections of the plan and build experts (never the Workflow), so the expert auto-updates its own knowledge." },
    { "q": "What's the difference between 'saving' and 'spending' tokens in Dan's framing?", "a": "The goal isn't minimizing tokens; it's spending them properly so you don't waste time/tokens correcting mistakes — enabling one-shot out-loop streaks so you can drop your presence." },
    { "q": "Name two future context-engineering trends Dan says to bet on.", "a": "Any two of: larger context windows; better (more effective) context windows; hot-swapped context; multi-agent architectures; specialized agents everywhere." }

    { "text": "A focused engineer is a performant engineer AND a focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "0:16", "source": "README + transcript (repeated as the lesson's refrain)" },
    { "text": "Your agent's context window is a precious, renewable, but limited temporal resource.", "approx_timestamp": "3:12" },
    { "text": "The context window is the single most important leverage point for effective agentic coding.", "approx_timestamp": "3:33" },
    { "text": "Search and destroy is the real skill in context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "2:41" },
    { "text": "When you boil it down, there are only two ways to manage your context window, R and D. Reduce and delegate.", "approx_timestamp": "2:55" },
    { "text": "What gets measured gets managed. So measure your context window.", "approx_timestamp": "5:25" },
    { "text": "If you aren't actively paying attention to the state of your agent's context, you're just vibe coding, and you'll only be able to tackle the lowest hanging fruit.", "approx_timestamp": "5:13" },
    { "text": "Do not load MCP servers unless you need them... it's very likely you're wasting tokens with MCP servers you're not actively using.", "approx_timestamp": "5:50" },
    { "text": "The CLAUDE.md file is incredible for one reason: it's a reusable memory file that's always loaded. Simultaneously, it's terrible for the exact same reason.", "approx_timestamp": "13:35" },
    { "text": "So prime, don't default. Your CLAUDE.md file should be shrunk to contain only the absolute universal essentials that you're 100% sure you want loaded 100% of the time.", "approx_timestamp": "14:55" },
    { "text": "Output tokens are priced anywhere from three to five X the price of your input tokens.", "approx_timestamp": "16:37" },
    { "text": "When you use Claude Code sub-agents, you are effectively creating a partially forked context window.", "approx_timestamp": "22:55" },
    { "text": "There's only two ways to manage your context window: reduce context entering your primary agent, and delegate context to sub-agents and to other primary agents.", "approx_timestamp": "26:20" },
    { "text": "By the end of your planning phase, you should be deleting information that isn't relevant to the work you want done. You should go overboard, then delete.", "approx_timestamp": "32:10" },
    { "text": "When you get to advanced agentic coding, it's time to stop guessing and start knowing. I avoid compact and I recommend that you reset and prime.", "approx_timestamp": "34:14" },
    { "text": "You don't want to delegate the control of your context window. You want to own this, just like you want to control your prompt or your model.", "approx_timestamp": "36:00" },
    { "text": "Use one agent for one purpose so that your context windows are focused. A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "42:50" },
    { "text": "The system prompt really lets you start controlling how your agent behaves, and when you control the behavior, you control the context window.", "approx_timestamp": "45:40" },
    { "text": "We are kicking off a Claude Code instance from Claude Code. We have compute orchestrating compute, agents orchestrating agents. This is where everything is headed. Better agents, and then more agents.", "approx_timestamp": "52:10" },
    { "text": "You fire off specialized agents that are experts at specific parts of your codebase, and here's the kicker, you have them auto-update their own knowledge. This is the agent experts technique.", "approx_timestamp": "57:34" },
    { "text": "It's not necessarily about saving tokens. It's about spending them properly. We manage our context window so that we don't waste time and tokens correcting our agents' mistakes.", "approx_timestamp": "68:38" },
    { "text": "It's a safe bet to bet on context engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "70:00" },
    { "text": "A focused agent is a performant agent.", "approx_timestamp": "73:08", "source": "sign-off" }

    { "q": "Why do custom sub-agents cost only ~122 tokens in the primary window?", "a": "A sub-agent's definition is a SYSTEM prompt, not a user prompt, so it isn't added to the primary agent's context window; the sub-agent burns its OWN window doing the work and returns a concise report to the primary agent." },
